6.1    Introduction: The First Mediation

The Hub of Decree is the mediating structure between the Category of First Determination
and the Category of Structural Determination. It is the first of the three Hubs, and it is the
first locus of refraction: the place where the pure unity of the First Determination becomes the
general multiplicity of the Structural Determination.

This chapter has six tasks. First, it explains the position and function of the Hub of Decree.
Second, it analyses its Barzakh-like nature. Third, it develops its two edges—the Transcendental
Edge and the Immanent Edge. Fourth, it analyses the refraction of unity into multiplicity. Fifth,
it develops the dynamism and rules of the Hub. Sixth, it introduces the ethics of measure—the
first of the three ethical mechanics of the Hubs.
78                                                                  Chapter 6. The Hub of Decree


6.2     Position and Function

6.2.1    The Position

The Hub of Decree stands between the Category of First Determination and the Category of
Structural Determination. It is the first of the three Hubs, and it is the first point at which the
pure unity of the First Determination begins to be differentiated.

The position of the Hub is not spatial; it is structural. It is the between—the transition between
two categories. It is not a category in its own right; it is the relation that connects two categories.



6.2.2    The Function

The function of the Hub of Decree is to measure the pure unity of the First Determination into
the class of allowable transformations. The word “Decree” (qadar ) is chosen deliberately: the
Hub does not create the structural laws; it measures the unity into a determinate structure.

The function of the Hub has three aspects.

First, it is a reception. The Hub receives the identity of the First Determination at its
Transcendental Edge. It does not receive the manifestations of the First Determination (there
are none); it receives the identity—the pure unity that the Hub will refract.

Second, it is a transformation. The Hub transforms the pure unity of the First Determina-
tion into the general multiplicity of the Structural Determination. The transformation is not a
loss; it is a specification. The unity is not diminished; it is expressed as the class of allowable
transformations.

Third, it is a transmission. The Hub transmits the general multiplicity of the Structural
Determination at its Immanent Edge. It does not transmit its own identity (the Hub has
no identity in its own right); it transmits the manifestation—the refracted form of the First
Determination’s identity.




6.3     The Barzakh-like Nature of the Hub of Decree

The most important feature of the Hub of Decree is its Barzakh-like nature. The general
definition was given in §4.3.4: a Hub is Barzakh-like if it possesses neither the full properties of
the higher category nor the full properties of the lower, but an incomplete mixture of both. We
apply this definition here to the first Hub.

The term “Barzakh” is drawn from the Islamic tradition, where it refers to the intermediate
realm between this world and the next—a realm that is neither fully material nor fully spiritual,
but a mixture of both. The Hub of Decree has an analogous nature: it possesses neither the
full unity of the First Determination nor the full multiplicity of the Structural Determination,
but an incomplete mixture of both.
6.4. The Transcendental Edge                                                                      79


6.3.1    On the Side of the First Determination

On the side of the First Determination, the Hub of Decree has unity: it is a single Hub, not a
plurality. It is the first mediation—the first point at which the pure unity of the First Determi-
nation begins to be differentiated. It retains a trace of the unity of the First Determination.

This trace of unity is what makes the Hub a Hub—a center, not a dispersal. The Hub is not
a mere boundary; it is a locus—a point at which unity is concentrated, even as it is being
differentiated.


6.3.2    On the Side of the Structural Determination

On the side of the Structural Determination, the Hub of Decree has multiplicity: it is the source
of the general multiplicity of the Structural Determination. It is the point at which the unity
of the First Determination is specified into the class of allowable transformations. It anticipates
the multiplicity of the Structural Determination.

This anticipation of multiplicity is what makes the Hub a prism—a locus of refraction, not a
mere conduit. The Hub does not merely transmit the unity; it transforms it, differentiating it
into the spectrum of structural laws.


6.3.3    Neither Fully Unity nor Fully Multiplicity

The Hub of Decree is neither fully unified nor fully multiple. It is the transition from unity to
multiplicity—a transition that partakes of both, but fully of neither. This is the Barzakh-like
nature of the Hub.

The Barzakh-like nature has three consequences. (The same three consequences apply to the
other two Hubs; we state them here once and cross-reference them in Chapters 8 and 10.)

First, the Hub is not a category. It is not a level of reality in its own right; it is the
transition between levels. It does not have its own mode of multiplicity; it has a mixture of the
multiplicities of the higher and lower categories.

Second, the Hub is not a substance. It is not a thing that exists independently; it is a
relation that connects the higher and lower categories. It is the “between”—the mediation that
makes the relation possible.

Third, the Hub is not a mere boundary. It is not a line that separates the higher and lower
categories; it is a zone of transition—a region in which the properties of the higher category are
gradually transformed into the properties of the lower category.



6.4     The Transcendental Edge

The Transcendental Edge of the Hub of Decree is the edge oriented toward the First Determi-
nation. Through this edge, the Hub receives the identity of the First Determination.
80                                                                 Chapter 6. The Hub of Decree


6.4.1    The Direction of Reception
The Transcendental Edge is oriented upward. It receives from the First Determination—from the
category that is above the Hub in the architectural order. The reception is not a passive reception;
it is an active reception—the Hub actively receives the identity of the First Determination and
prepares it for refraction.

The reception can be understood by analogy. Consider a lens. The lens receives light from a
source; it does not passively let the light pass through, but actively refracts it—it bends the
light, focuses it, transforms it. Similarly, the Transcendental Edge of the Hub of Decree receives
the identity of the First Determination and actively prepares it for refraction.


6.4.2    The Nature of the Reception
The reception through the Transcendental Edge is a reception of identity, not of manifestation.
The First Determination does not transmit its manifestations to the Hub (there are none); it
transmits its identity—the pure unity that the Hub will refract into the Structural Determina-
tion.

This is a crucial point. If the First Determination transmitted its manifestations, the Hub would
be redundant—the manifestations would already be formed, and the Hub would have nothing
to do. But the First Determination transmits its identity—its pure, unrefracted unity—and the
Hub’s task is to refract this unity into the multiplicity of the Structural Determination.


6.4.3    The Barzakh-like Nature of the Transcendental Edge
The Transcendental Edge is Barzakh-like in its own way: it is neither fully of the First Determi-
nation nor fully of the Hub, but the transition between them. It is the point at which the identity
of the First Determination enters the Hub—the threshold between the First Determination and
the Hub.

This means that the Transcendental Edge is not a sharp boundary; it is a zone of transition.
The identity of the First Determination does not suddenly become the Hub; it gradually enters
the Hub, becoming more and more refracted as it passes through the edge. The edge is the
process of entry, not a static line.


6.5     The Immanent Edge
The Immanent Edge of the Hub of Decree is the edge oriented toward the Structural Determina-
tion. Through this edge, the Hub transmits the manifestation to the Structural Determination.


6.5.1    The Direction of Transmission
The Immanent Edge is oriented downward. It transmits to the Structural Determination—to
the category that is below the Hub in the architectural order. The transmission is not a passive
transmission; it is an active transmission—the Hub actively transmits the refracted manifestation
to the Structural Determination.
6.6. The Refraction of Unity into Multiplicity                                                 81


The transmission can be understood by analogy. Consider a prism. The prism receives white
light at one face; it emits a spectrum at the other face. The emission is not a passive letting-
through; it is an active transformation—the prism transforms the white light into a spectrum.
Similarly, the Immanent Edge of the Hub of Decree transmits the refracted manifestation to the
Structural Determination—it is the point at which the Hub’s transformation is completed and
the result is transmitted to the lower category.


6.5.2       The Nature of the Transmission

The transmission through the Immanent Edge is a transmission of manifestation, not of identity.
The Hub does not transmit its identity to the Structural Determination (the Hub has no identity
in its own right); it transmits the manifestation—the refracted form of the First Determination’s
identity.

This is a crucial point. If the Hub transmitted its identity, the Structural Determination would
be a copy of the Hub, not a manifestation of the First Determination. But the Hub transmits
its manifestation—the refracted form of the First Determination’s identity—and the Structural
Determination’s task is to receive this manifestation and to manifest it in its own mode.


6.5.3       The Barzakh-like Nature of the Immanent Edge

The Immanent Edge is Barzakh-like in its own way: it is neither fully of the Hub nor fully of
the Structural Determination, but the transition between them. It is the point at which the
manifestation of the Hub enters the Structural Determination—the threshold between the Hub
and the lower category.

This means that the Immanent Edge is not a sharp boundary; it is a zone of transition. The
manifestation of the Hub does not suddenly become the Structural Determination; it gradually
enters the Structural Determination, becoming more and more specified as it passes through the
edge. The edge is the process of exit, not a static line.



6.6     The Refraction of Unity into Multiplicity

6.6.1       The Nature of Refraction

The Hub of Decree refracts the pure unity of the First Determination into the general multi-
plicity of the Structural Determination. This refraction is a specification: the pure unity is not
diminished; it is expressed as the class of allowable transformations.

The refraction can be understood by analogy. Consider a white light passing through a prism.
The white light is a unity—it contains all colors, but they are not differentiated. When the light
passes through the prism, it is refracted into a spectrum—a multiplicity of colors. The spectrum
is not the white light; it is the white light specified into its component colors. Similarly, the
Hub of Decree refracts the pure unity of the First Determination into the general multiplicity
of the Structural Determination—the specification of the unity into the structural laws.
82                                                                 Chapter 6. The Hub of Decree


6.6.2    The Dynamism of Measurement

The dynamism of the Hub of Decree is the dynamism of measurement. It is the act by which
the pure unity of the First Determination is measured into a determinate structure.

The dynamism of measurement has three aspects.

First, it is an act of specification. The Hub does not merely receive the unity; it speci-
fies it. It specifies the unity into the class of allowable transformations—it determines what
transformations the identity tolerates.

Second, it is an act of proportion. The Hub does not specify arbitrarily; it specifies
proportionately. The specification must preserve the unity of the First Determination even as
it differentiates it. This is why the ethics of measure (see §6.7) is the first of the three ethical
mechanics of the Hubs.

Third, it is an act of ordering. The Hub does not specify chaotically; it specifies orderly.
The specification must follow the structure of the categories. This is why the Hub is called the
Hub of Decree (qadar ): it decrees the measure of things, and the measure is ordered.


6.6.3    The Rules of the Hub

The rules of the Hub of Decree are the structural constraints that govern its mode of being.
They are three.

Rule One: Proportion. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be proportionate.
The specification must preserve the unity of the First Determination even as it differentiates
it. An over-specification (multiplication without unity) or an under-specification (unity without
multiplicity) is a violation of the rule of proportion.

Rule Two: Order. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be ordered. The specifica-
tion must follow the structure of the categories—the higher before the lower, the general before
the particular. A disorderly specification (confusing the higher and the lower) is a violation of
the rule of order.

Rule Three: Harmony. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be harmonious.
The specification must produce a multiplicity that is coherent, not chaotic. A disharmonious
specification (multiplication without coherence) is a violation of the rule of harmony.

These three rules are not separate; they are three aspects of a single structural constraint. The
Hub of Decree is proportionate because it is ordered, ordered because it is harmonious. The three
rules are the articulation of the Hub’s dynamism.


6.7     The Ethics of Measure

6.7.1    The Ethical Function of the Hub

The ethical function of the Hub of Decree is the ethics of measure. It is the discipline of ensuring
that the passage from unity to multiplicity is proportionate—that the specification of unity into
6.8. Objections and Replies                                                                    83


multiplicity is not distorted by excess or deficiency.

The ethics of measure is the first of the three ethical mechanics of the Hubs (the other two are
the ethics of meaning, in Chapter 8, and the ethics of manifestation, in Chapter 10). The full
development of these mechanics is given in Chapter 26. Here we introduce the first of them.


6.7.2    The Three Dimensions of the Ethics of Measure

The ethics of measure has three dimensions.

First, the dimension of proportion. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be
proportionate—it must preserve the unity while expressing the multiplicity. An action that
over-specifies (that multiplies without preserving unity) is disproportionate. An action that
under-specifies (that preserves unity without expressing multiplicity) is also disproportionate.

Second, the dimension of order. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be
ordered—it must follow the structure of the categories. An action that violates the order of
the categories (that confuses the higher and the lower) is disorderly.

Third, the dimension of harmony. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be
harmonious—it must produce a multiplicity that is coherent, not chaotic. An action that pro-
duces chaos (that multiplies without coherence) is disharmonious.


6.7.3    The Traditional Name: Temperance

The ethics of measure is known in the traditional vocabulary as temperance—the virtue of
moderation, the avoidance of excess and deficiency. The framework adopts this traditional name,
but transposes it into a structural key. Temperance is not merely a psychological disposition; it
is a structural rule of the Hub of Decree. The temperate person is the one who specifies their
identity into their manifestations proportionately, orderly, and harmoniously.

The ethical implications of the ethics of measure are developed in Chapter 26. For now, we note
that the ethics of measure is not a set of arbitrary rules; it is the structural condition for the
safe passage of ascending light through the Immanent Edge of the Hub of Decree.


6.8     Objections and Replies
Objection 6.1. The term “Hub” is unfamiliar in philosophy. Why not use a more standard
term, like “mediator” or “intermediary”?

Reply 6.1. The term “Hub” is chosen because it captures the specific nature of the mediating
structures. A “mediator” is too general—it could refer to any kind of mediation. An “intermedi-
ary” is too passive—it suggests a passive go-between, not an active locus of transformation. A
“Hub” is active, central, and transformative—it is a point through which many lines pass, and
at which the flow is redirected and transformed. This is precisely what the Hub of Decree is.

Objection 6.2. The Barzakh-like nature of the Hub is a theological concept, not a philosophical
one.
84                                                                   Chapter 6. The Hub of Decree


Reply 6.2. The Barzakh-like nature of the Hub is a structural concept, not a theological one. It
describes the nature of a transition—a transition that partakes of both sides, but fully of neither.
This structure is found in many domains: the transition from solid to liquid, the transition from
sleeping to waking, the transition from unity to multiplicity. The term “Barzakh” is borrowed
from the Islamic tradition because it is a vivid name for this structure, but the structure itself
is universal.

Objection 6.3. If the Hub is Barzakh-like, then it is ambiguous and cannot be known.

Reply 6.3. The Hub is ambiguous, but it is not unknowable. It can be known through its
effects—through the specification of unity into multiplicity. We cannot observe the Hub of
Decree directly, but we can observe the specification of unity into multiplicity. The Hub is
known through its effects, not through direct observation.

Objection 6.4. Why is the Hub of Decree called “Decree”? Is this not a theological term?

Reply 6.4. The word “Decree” (qadar ) is chosen because it captures the specific function of the
Hub: it measures the unity into a determinate structure. The Hub does not create the structural
laws; it measures them. “Decree” is a vivid name for this act of measurement, drawn from the
Islamic tradition where qadar means “measure” or “decree.” The framework uses the term as a
structural description, not as a theological doctrine.

Objection 6.5. The ethics of measure seems to be a form of naturalism—it derives ethics from
the structure of the Hub.

Reply 6.5. The ethics of measure is not a form of naturalism. It does not derive ethics from
the structure of the Hub; it discovers ethics in the structure of the Hub. The distinction is
crucial: naturalism derives “ought” from “is”; the ethics of measure discovers “ought” in the
same structure in which “is” is discovered. The structure is both descriptive and normative—not
because description entails normativity, but because the structure itself is the locus of both.


6.9     Conclusion: The First Locus of Refraction
The Hub of Decree is the first locus of refraction. It receives the pure unity of the First
Determination at its Transcendental Edge, and emits the general multiplicity of the Structural
Determination at its Immanent Edge. It does not create the structural laws; it measures the
unity into a determinate structure.

We have seen that the Hub is Barzakh-like—neither fully unity nor fully multiplicity. We have
seen that its two edges are zones of transition, not static boundaries. We have seen that its
dynamism is the dynamism of measurement, and that its rules are proportion, order, and har-
mony. We have seen that its ethical function is the ethics of measure—known in the traditional
vocabulary as temperance.

The next chapter will develop the Category of Structural Determination—the realm of general
multiplicity, the realm of the class of allowable transformations.

Keywords: Structural Determination, General Multiplicity, Allowable Transformations, Struc-
tural Laws, Universality, Necessity, Lawfulness, Formal Sciences, Dynamism of Unfolding.




7.1    Introduction: The Realm of General Multiplicity

The Category of Structural Determination is the second of the four categories. It is the realm of
the class of allowable transformations—the structural laws that govern how identity can manifest.
In this category, multiplicity is general, not particular. The laws are universal, not contextual.
They apply to all manifestations of a given identity, regardless of context.

This chapter has five tasks. First, it describes the nature of the Category of Structural Deter-
mination. Second, it develops its dynamism—the dynamism of unfolding. Third, it sets out
the rules that govern it. Fourth, it analyses its relation to the Hub of Decree and the Hub
of Signification. Fifth, it discusses the formal sciences, which are the paradigm case of this
category.
86                                        Chapter 7. The Category of Structural Determination


7.2     The Nature of the Category

7.2.1    The Realm of Allowable Transformations
In Chapter 1, we defined identity as that which remains invariant under a specified class of
allowable transformations. The Category of Structural Determination is the realm of this class.
It is the level at which the pure unity of the First Determination is specified —differentiated into
the structural laws that determine what transformations are allowable.

The Category of Structural Determination is not directly accessible to observation. It is the
structure that underlies all manifestations, but it is not itself a manifestation. It is known
through its effects—through the patterns of invariance that can be detected in the manifestations.
The mathematician does not observe the laws of mathematics; they discover them through the
study of particular mathematical objects. The logician does not observe the laws of logic; they
discover them through the study of particular arguments. Similarly, the Category of Structural
Determination is known through its effects, not through direct observation.


7.2.2    The Generality of Multiplicity
The multiplicity of the Category of Structural Determination is general. This means that the
laws are universal—they apply to all manifestations of a given identity, regardless of context.
The laws of mathematics are the same for all mathematical objects; the laws of logic are the
same for all arguments; the laws of physics (if we take them as structural laws) are the same for
all physical systems.

This generality is what distinguishes the Structural Determination from the Relational Man-
ifestation. In the Relational Manifestation, multiplicity is relational —the manifestations are
connected to one another through relations of meaning, value, and significance, and these re-
lations are context-dependent. In the Structural Determination, multiplicity is general —the
manifestations are governed by universal laws that do not depend on context.

The distinction is important. It means that the Structural Determination is the realm of neces-
sity, while the Relational Manifestation is the realm of contingency. The laws of the Structural
Determination are necessary—they could not be otherwise, given the identity they express. The
relations of the Relational Manifestation are contingent—they depend on the context in which
they occur.


7.3     The Dynamism of Unfolding
The dynamism of the Category of Structural Determination is the dynamism of unfolding. It is
the unfolding of the structural laws into their consequences.

The dynamism of unfolding has three aspects.

First, it is an unfolding of implication. The structural laws imply their consequences. From
the axioms of a mathematical system, the theorems follow by logical implication. From the laws
of a physical system, the behavior of the system follows by causal implication. This unfolding
7.4. The Relation to the Hub of Decree                                                             87


is the dynamism of the Structural Determination: it is the movement from law to consequence.

Second, it is an unfolding of universality. The structural laws apply universally, but
their application unfolds in a multiplicity of instances. The law of non-contradiction applies
universally, but its application unfolds in a multiplicity of particular arguments. The law of
gravity applies universally, but its application unfolds in a multiplicity of particular trajectories.
This unfolding is the dynamism of the Structural Determination: it is the movement from
universality to multiplicity.

Third, it is an unfolding of necessity. The structural laws are necessary, and their unfolding
is necessary. Given the laws, the consequences could not be otherwise. This is why the Structural
Determination is the realm of necessity: its dynamism is not a free creation, but a necessary
unfolding.


7.3.1    The Rules of the Category

The rules of the Category of Structural Determination are the structural constraints that govern
its mode of being. They are three.

Rule One: Universality. The structural laws are universal. They apply to all manifestations
of a given identity, regardless of context. A law that applies only in some contexts is not a
structural law; it is a relational regularity.

Rule Two: Necessity. The structural laws are necessary. They could not be otherwise, given
the identity they express. A law that could be otherwise is not a structural law; it is a contingent
regularity.

Rule Three: Formality. The structural laws are formal. They concern the form of the
manifestations, not their content. The law of non-contradiction concerns the form of arguments,
not their subject matter. The law of gravity concerns the form of trajectories, not the nature of
the bodies. A law that concerns content is not a structural law; it is a material law.

These three rules are not separate; they are three aspects of a single structural constraint. The
Structural Determination is universal because it is necessary, necessary because it is formal. The
three rules are the articulation of the category’s nature.


7.4     The Relation to the Hub of Decree
The Category of Structural Determination is a manifestation of the Category of First Determina-
tion, mediated by the Hub of Decree (Chapter 6). It is the first level of refraction: the pure light
of identity is refracted by the Hub into the structural laws that determine what transformations
are allowable.

This refraction is not a loss; it is a specification. The Category of First Determination is pure
unity; the Category of Structural Determination is general multiplicity. The one becomes many,
but the many are still general, not particular. The laws apply universally, not contextually.

The relation between the First Determination and the Structural Determination can be under-
88                                        Chapter 7. The Category of Structural Determination


stood by analogy. Consider a geometrical figure—say, a triangle. The triangle, in its pure form,
is a unity: it is one figure, with one essence. But when we specify the triangle—when we say
that it has three sides, three angles, and a specific area—we introduce multiplicity. The three
sides, the three angles, the area—these are the specifications of the triangle. They are not the
triangle itself, but they are not other than the triangle; they are the triangle in its specified
form.

Similarly, the Category of First Determination is the pure unity of identity. The Category of
Structural Determination is the specification of this unity into the structural laws that govern
manifestation. The laws are not the identity itself, but they are not other than the identity;
they are the identity in its specified form.


7.5     The Relation to the Hub of Signification
The Category of Structural Determination is the environment of the Category of Relational Man-
ifestation, and is encompassed by the Category of First Determination. Between the Structural
Determination and the Relational Manifestation stands the Hub of Signification (Chapter 8).

The Hub of Signification receives the general multiplicity of the Structural Determination at
its Transcendental Edge, and emits the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation
at its Immanent Edge. The Hub’s function is to contextualize the general laws into particular
meanings.

The relation between the Structural Determination and the Hub of Signification is a relation
of transmission. The Structural Determination transmits its manifestation—the general mul-
tiplicity of the structural laws—to the Hub, which then contextualizes it into the relational
multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation.

The Category of Structural Determination has two edges: a Transcendental Edge oriented to the
Hub of Decree (the Hub above it), and an Immanent Edge oriented to the Hub of Signification
(the Hub below it). It receives from the Hub of Decree through its Transcendental Edge, and it
transmits to the Hub of Signification through its Immanent Edge.


7.6     The Formal Sciences

7.6.1    The Paradigm Case

The formal sciences—mathematics, logic, and the formal parts of computer science—are the
paradigm case of the Category of Structural Determination. They are the disciplines that study
the structural laws in their purest form, without reference to particular contexts or particular
contents.

The mathematician studies the laws of mathematical structures—the patterns of invariance that
govern mathematical objects. The logician studies the laws of logical structures—the patterns
of invariance that govern arguments. The computer scientist studies the laws of computational
structures—the patterns of invariance that govern computation.
7.7. Objections and Replies                                                                     89


In each case, the formal scientist is studying the Category of Structural Determination. The laws
they discover are not empirical generalizations; they are structural laws—necessary, universal,
and formal.


7.6.2    The Relation to the Relational Manifestation
The formal sciences are not the whole of the Structural Determination. They are the paradigm
case, but there are other cases. The laws of physics, for example, are also structural laws—
they are necessary, universal, and formal (in the sense that they concern the form of physical
processes, not their content).

But the formal sciences have a special relation to the Relational Manifestation. The formal
sciences study the structural laws in their purity; the Relational Manifestation studies the con-
textual meanings that arise when these laws are applied in particular contexts. The formal
sciences are the form; the Relational Manifestation is the content.

This is why the Hub of Signification is the bridge between the two. The Hub contextualizes the
general laws into particular meanings. The formal sciences are the general laws; the Relational
Manifestation is the particular meanings.


7.7     Objections and Replies
Objection 7.1. The Category of Structural Determination seems to be a form of Platonism—it
posits a realm of abstract structures that exist independently of the material world.

Reply 7.1. The Category of Structural Determination is not a form of Platonism. Platon-
ism posits a realm of abstract objects that exist independently of the material world. The
framework’s Structural Determination is not a realm of abstract objects; it is a level of a single
reality—the level at which identity is specified into structural laws. The laws are not independent
entities; they are the specification of identity at a particular level of refraction.

Objection 7.2. If the Structural Determination is the realm of necessity, how can there be
freedom?

Reply 7.2. The Structural Determination is the realm of necessity at the level of structure,
but freedom is possible at the level of reconstruction. The subject is determined at the level
of structure (it must operate within the constraints imposed by the identity’s structure), but
free at the level of reconstruction (it may choose which manifestations to attend to, which
approximations to construct, which costs to bear, and when to revise). This is the compatibilist
position that will be developed in Chapter 19.

Objection 7.3. The distinction between Structural Determination and Relational Manifesta-
tion seems arbitrary. Why separate them?

Reply 7.3. The distinction is not arbitrary; it is structural. The Structural Determination is the
realm of general multiplicity—the laws apply universally, regardless of context. The Relational
Manifestation is the realm of relational multiplicity—the meanings are context-dependent. The
two realms are distinct because they have different modes of multiplicity. The distinction is
90                                        Chapter 7. The Category of Structural Determination


necessary to account for the difference between the formal sciences (which study universal laws)
and the human sciences (which study contextual meanings).

Objection 7.4. The formal sciences do not exhaust the Category of Structural Determination.
What about the laws of physics?

Reply 7.4. The formal sciences are the paradigm case of the Category of Structural Deter-
mination, not its exhaustive content. The laws of physics are also structural laws—they are
necessary, universal, and formal. The framework includes them in the Category of Structural
Determination, even though they are not studied by the formal sciences in the narrow sense.


7.8    Conclusion: The Realm of General Multiplicity
The Category of Structural Determination is the realm of the class of allowable transformations.
It is the realm of structural laws—the patterns of invariance that govern how identity can
manifest. In this category, multiplicity is general, not particular; the laws are universal, not
contextual.

We have seen that the Structural Determination is the realm of general multiplicity, distinguished
from the Relational Manifestation by its mode of multiplicity. We have seen that its dynamism
is the dynamism of unfolding—the unfolding of law into consequence. We have seen that its
rules are universality, necessity, and formality. We have seen that its relation to the Hub of
Decree is a relation of specification, and its relation to the Hub of Signification is a relation of
transmission. And we have seen that the formal sciences are the paradigm case of this category.

The next chapter will develop the Hub of Signification—the mediating structure between the
Structural Determination and the Relational Manifestation.

8.1     Introduction: The Second Mediation


The Hub of Signification is the mediating structure between the Category of Structural Deter-
mination and the Category of Relational Manifestation. It is the second of the three Hubs, and
it is the second locus of refraction: the place where the general multiplicity of the Structural
Determination becomes the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation.

This chapter has six tasks. First, it explains the position and function of the Hub of Signification.
Second, it analyses its Barzakh-like nature. Third, it develops its two edges. Fourth, it analyses
the refraction of generality into relationality. Fifth, it develops the dynamism and rules of the
Hub. Sixth, it introduces the ethics of meaning—the second of the three ethical mechanics of
the Hubs.
92                                                            Chapter 8. The Hub of Signification


8.2     Position and Function

8.2.1    The Position
The Hub of Signification stands between the Category of Structural Determination and the Cat-
egory of Relational Manifestation. It is the second of the three Hubs, and it is the second point
at which the general multiplicity of the Structural Determination begins to be contextualized.

The position of the Hub is not spatial; it is structural. It is the between—the transition between
two categories. It is not a category in its own right; it is the relation that connects two categories.


8.2.2    The Function
The function of the Hub of Signification is to signify the general multiplicity of the Structural
Determination into the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation. The word “Signi-
fication” is chosen deliberately: the Hub does not create meaning; it signifies the structure into
a context.

The function of the Hub has three aspects.

First, it is a reception. The Hub receives the general multiplicity of the Structural Determina-
tion at its Transcendental Edge. It does not receive the identity of the Structural Determination;
it receives the manifestation—the general multiplicity of the structural laws.

Second, it is a transformation. The Hub transforms the general multiplicity of the Structural
Determination into the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation. The transforma-
tion is not a loss; it is a contextualization. The general laws are not diminished; they are expressed
as context-dependent meanings.

Third, it is a transmission. The Hub transmits the relational multiplicity of the Relational
Manifestation at its Immanent Edge. It does not transmit its own identity (the Hub has no iden-
tity in its own right); it transmits the manifestation—the contextualized form of the Structural
Determination’s manifestation.


8.3     The Barzakh-like Nature of the Hub of Signification
The most important feature of the Hub of Signification is its Barzakh-like nature. The definition
and the three consequences are given in §4.3.4 and §6.3; we apply them here to the second Hub.

The Hub has an analogous nature to the barzakh of the Islamic tradition: it is neither fully of
the higher category nor fully of the lower, but an incomplete mixture of both.


8.3.1    On the Side of the Structural Determination
On the side of the Structural Determination, the Hub of Signification has generality: it is
the point at which the universal laws of the Structural Determination are signified —given a
determinate form. It retains a trace of the generality of the Structural Determination.

This trace of generality is what makes the Hub a Hub—a center, not a dispersal. The Hub is
8.4. The Transcendental Edge                                                                    93


not a mere boundary; it is a locus—a point at which generality is concentrated, even as it is
being contextualized.


8.3.2    On the Side of the Relational Manifestation
On the side of the Relational Manifestation, the Hub of Signification has relationality: it is the
source of the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation. It is the point at which the
universal laws are contextualized into meanings. It anticipates the relationality of the Relational
Manifestation.

This anticipation of relationality is what makes the Hub a prism—a locus of refraction, not a
mere conduit. The Hub does not merely transmit the generality; it transforms it, contextualizing
it into the spectrum of meanings.


8.3.3    Neither Fully Generality nor Fully Relationality
The Hub of Signification is neither fully general nor fully relational. It is the transition from
generality to relationality—a transition that partakes of both, but fully of neither. This is the
Barzakh-like nature of the Hub.

The three consequences stated in §6.3 apply here mutatis mutandis: the Hub is not a category,
not a substance, not a mere boundary; it is a zone of transition.


8.4     The Transcendental Edge
The Transcendental Edge of the Hub of Signification is the edge oriented toward the Struc-
tural Determination. Through this edge, the Hub receives the manifestation of the Structural
Determination.

The Transcendental Edge is oriented upward. It receives from the Structural Determination—
from the category that is above the Hub in the architectural order. The reception is not a
passive reception; it is an active reception—the Hub actively receives the manifestation of the
Structural Determination and prepares it for contextualization.

The nature of the reception is the same as in the Hub of Decree (§6.4): the Hub receives the
manifestation of the higher category, not its identity. The Structural Determination does not
transmit its identity to the Hub; it transmits its manifestation—the general multiplicity of the
structural laws.


8.5     The Immanent Edge
The Immanent Edge of the Hub of Signification is the edge oriented toward the Relational
Manifestation. Through this edge, the Hub transmits the manifestation to the Relational Man-
ifestation.

The Immanent Edge is oriented downward. It transmits to the Relational Manifestation—to
the category that is below the Hub in the architectural order. The transmission is not a pas-
94                                                            Chapter 8. The Hub of Signification


sive transmission; it is an active transmission—the Hub actively transmits the contextualized
manifestation to the Relational Manifestation.

The nature of the transmission is the same as in the Hub of Decree (§6.5): the Hub transmits
the manifestation of the higher category, not its own identity. The Relational Manifestation
receives the manifestation—the relational multiplicity of meanings.


8.6     The Refraction of Generality into Relationality

8.6.1    The Nature of Refraction
The Hub of Signification refracts the general multiplicity of the Structural Determination into
the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation. This refraction is a contextualization:
the universal laws are not diminished; they are expressed as context-dependent meanings.

The refraction can be understood by analogy. Consider the word “bank.” As a structural unit
(a pattern of letters), it is general—it could mean a financial institution, the side of a river, or a
tilt of an aircraft. But when the word is used in a specific context—say, “I went to the bank to
deposit my paycheck”—it is signified as meaning “financial institution.” The structural unit is
general; the meaning is contextual. The Hub of Signification is the point at which the general
becomes contextual—the point at which the structural unit is signified as a specific meaning.


8.6.2    The Dynamism of Signification
The dynamism of the Hub of Signification is the dynamism of signification. It is the act by
which the general multiplicity of the Structural Determination is signified into a determinate
meaning.

The dynamism of signification has three aspects.

First, it is an act of contextualization. The Hub does not merely receive the generality; it
contextualizes it. It contextualizes the generality into the relational multiplicity of meanings—it
determines what the generality means in a particular context.

Second, it is an act of accuracy. The Hub does not contextualize arbitrarily; it contextualizes
accurately. The contextualization must preserve the structure of the Structural Determination
even as it differentiates it into meanings. This is why the ethics of meaning (see §8.7) is the
second of the three ethical mechanics of the Hubs.

Third, it is an act of fidelity. The Hub does not contextualize deceptively; it contextualizes
faithfully. The contextualization must be faithful to the structure of the Structural Determina-
tion. This is why the Hub is called the Hub of Signification: it signifies the structure into a
context, and the signification must be faithful.


8.6.3    The Rules of the Hub
The rules of the Hub of Signification are the structural constraints that govern its mode of being.
They are three.
8.7. The Ethics of Meaning                                                                           95


Rule One: Truthfulness. The signification of structure into meaning must be truthful. The
signification must represent the structure as it is, not as we wish it to be. A false signification
(signifying a meaning that is not faithful to the structure) is a violation of the rule of truthfulness.

Rule Two: Accuracy. The signification of structure into meaning must be accurate. The
signification must be precise, not vague. An inaccurate signification (signifying a meaning that
is not precise) is a violation of the rule of accuracy.

Rule Three: Fidelity. The signification of structure into meaning must be faithful. The
signification must preserve the structure through the signification. A betrayal of the structure
(signifying a meaning that is unfaithful to the structure) is a violation of the rule of fidelity.

These three rules are not separate; they are three aspects of a single structural constraint. The
Hub of Signification is truthful because it is accurate, accurate because it is faithful. The three
rules are the articulation of the Hub’s dynamism.


8.7     The Ethics of Meaning

8.7.1    The Ethical Function of the Hub

The ethical function of the Hub of Signification is the ethics of meaning. It is the discipline
of ensuring that the passage from structure to meaning is truthful —that the signification of
structure into meaning is not distorted by deception or error.

The ethics of meaning is the second of the three ethical mechanics of the Hubs. The full
development is given in Chapter 26. Here we introduce the second of them.


8.7.2    The Three Dimensions of the Ethics of Meaning

The ethics of meaning has three dimensions.

First, the dimension of truthfulness. The signification of structure into meaning must
be truthful—it must represent the structure as it is. A false signification (misrepresenting the
structure) is untruthful.

Second, the dimension of accuracy. The signification of structure into meaning must be
accurate—it must be precise, not vague. An inaccurate signification (misrepresenting the struc-
ture in detail) is inaccurate.

Third, the dimension of fidelity. The signification of structure into meaning must be
faithful—it must preserve the structure through the signification. A betrayal of the structure
(signifying a meaning that is unfaithful to the structure) is unfaithful.


8.7.3    The Traditional Name: Truthfulness

The ethics of meaning is known in the traditional vocabulary as truthfulness—the virtue of
honesty, the avoidance of deception and error. The framework adopts this traditional name, but
transposes it into a structural key. Truthfulness is not merely a psychological disposition; it is
96                                                           Chapter 8. The Hub of Signification


a structural rule of the Hub of Signification. The truthful person is the one who signifies their
identity into their manifestations truthfully, accurately, and faithfully.

The ethical implications of the ethics of meaning are developed in Chapter 26. For now, we note
that the ethics of meaning is not a set of arbitrary rules; it is the structural condition for the
safe passage of ascending light through the Immanent Edge of the Hub of Signification.


8.8     Objections and Replies
Objection 8.1. The Hub of Signification seems to conflate two different things: the structure
of a sign and its meaning.

Reply 8.1. The Hub of Signification does not conflate these two things; it relates them. The
structure of a sign (its form) is the contribution of the Structural Determination. The meaning of
a sign (its content) is the contribution of the Relational Manifestation. The Hub is the mediating
structure that connects the two. It is not the sign itself; it is the process by which the sign is
signified as meaning.

Objection 8.2. If the Hub is Barzakh-like, then it is ambiguous and cannot be known.

Reply 8.2. The Hub is ambiguous, but it is not unknowable. It can be known through its
effects—through the contextualization of generality into meaning. We cannot observe the Hub
of Signification directly, but we can observe the contextualization of generality into meaning.
The Hub is known through its effects, not through direct observation.

Objection 8.3. The ethics of meaning seems to be a form of moral realism, which is controver-
sial.

Reply 8.3. The ethics of meaning is indeed a form of moral realism, but it is a structural
realism, not a property realism. It does not claim that moral properties exist independently of
all contexts; it claims that the structure of the Hub of Signification is real, and that the ethics
of meaning is the discovery of this structure. This is a form of realism that is compatible with
the fallibilist epistemology of the framework.

Objection 8.4. The traditional name “truthfulness” seems too narrow for the ethics of meaning.
Truthfulness is only one of the three dimensions.

Reply 8.4. The traditional name “truthfulness” is retained because it captures the central di-
mension of the ethics of meaning. But the ethics of meaning has three dimensions—truthfulness,
accuracy, and fidelity—and the framework uses the traditional name as a shorthand for all three.
The ethics of meaning is the discipline of truthfulness, accuracy, and fidelity in the signification
of structure into meaning.


8.9     Conclusion: The Second Locus of Refraction
The Hub of Signification is the second locus of refraction. It receives the general multiplicity of
the Structural Determination at its Transcendental Edge, and emits the relational multiplicity
of the Relational Manifestation at its Immanent Edge. It does not create meaning; it signifies
8.9. Conclusion: The Second Locus of Refraction                                                97


the structure into a context.

We have seen that the Hub is Barzakh-like—neither fully generality nor fully relationality. We
have seen that its two edges are zones of transition, not static boundaries. We have seen that
its dynamism is the dynamism of signification, and that its rules are truthfulness, accuracy, and
fidelity. We have seen that its ethical function is the ethics of meaning—known in the traditional
vocabulary as truthfulness.

The next chapter will develop the Category of Relational Manifestation—the realm of meaning,
consciousness, and self-awareness.

Keywords: Relational Manifestation, Relational Multiplicity, Meaning, Consciousness, Self-

9.1      Introduction: The Realm of Meaning and Consciousness

The Category of Relational Manifestation is the third of the four categories. It is the realm
of meaning and consciousness—the realm of awareness, relationship, and significance. In this
category, multiplicity is relational : manifestations are connected to one another through relations
of meaning, value, and significance.

This chapter has five tasks. First, it describes the nature of the Category of Relational Man-
ifestation. Second, it develops its dynamism—the dynamism of relation. Third, it introduces
the three-fold distinction between self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness (which will be
developed fully in Chapter 19). Fourth, it sets out the rules that govern it. Fifth, it analyses its
relations to the Hub of Signification and the Hub of Realization.
9.2. The Nature of the Category                                                                99


9.2     The Nature of the Category

9.2.1   The Realm of Meaning
The Category of Relational Manifestation is the realm of meaning. Meaning is not a property of
individual manifestations; it is a relation between manifestations. A word has meaning because it
is connected to other words, to objects, to contexts, to speakers. A gesture has meaning because
it is connected to other gestures, to intentions, to social conventions. Meaning is relational; it
emerges from the network of relations among manifestations.

The Category of Relational Manifestation is also the realm of consciousness. Consciousness is
the reflective light within this category—the awareness of other manifestations within the same
category. (This will be developed in Chapter 13.) Consciousness is not a substance; it is a
process—the process by which manifestations become aware of one another.

9.2.2   The Relational Multiplicity
The multiplicity of the Category of Relational Manifestation is relational. This means that the
manifestations are connected to one another through relations of meaning, value, and significance,
and these relations are context-dependent. The meaning of a word depends on its context; the
significance of a gesture depends on its social setting; the value of an action depends on its
circumstances.

This relational multiplicity is what distinguishes the Relational Manifestation from the Struc-
tural Determination. In the Structural Determination, multiplicity is general—the laws are
universal, regardless of context. In the Relational Manifestation, multiplicity is relational—the
meanings are context-dependent, relative to the network of relations in which they occur.


9.3     The Dynamism of Relation
The dynamism of the Category of Relational Manifestation is the dynamism of relation. It is
the unfolding of meaning through the network of relations among manifestations.

The dynamism of relation has three aspects.

First, it is an unfolding of connection. The dynamism of the Relational Manifestation
is not the unfolding of a law (as in the Structural Determination); it is the unfolding of a
connection. Manifestations become connected to one another, and through this connection,
meaning emerges. This unfolding is the dynamism of the Relational Manifestation: it is the
movement from isolation to relation.

Second, it is an unfolding of context. The dynamism of the Relational Manifestation is
not the unfolding of a universal law; it is the unfolding of a particular context. The meaning of
a manifestation depends on its context, and the context unfolds as the manifestation is related
to other manifestations. This unfolding is the dynamism of the Relational Manifestation: it is
the movement from abstract to concrete.

Third, it is an unfolding of awareness. The dynamism of the Relational Manifestation is
100                                        Chapter 9. The Category of Relational Manifestation


not the unfolding of a formal structure; it is the unfolding of awareness. Manifestations become
aware of one another, and through this awareness, consciousness emerges. This unfolding is the
dynamism of the Relational Manifestation: it is the movement from unawareness to awareness.


9.3.1    The Rules of the Category
The rules of the Category of Relational Manifestation are the structural constraints that govern
its mode of being. They are three.

Rule One: Relationality. The manifestations of the Relational Manifestation are relational.
They exist only in relation to one another; they have no independent existence. A manifestation
that is not related to any other is not a manifestation of the Relational Manifestation; it is a
mere isolated event.

Rule Two: Contextuality. The manifestations of the Relational Manifestation are contextual.
Their meaning depends on their context; it is not fixed independently of the context. A manifes-
tation that has a fixed meaning, regardless of context, is not a manifestation of the Relational
Manifestation; it is a mere structural unit.

Rule Three: Awareness. The manifestations of the Relational Manifestation are aware.
They are not merely related to one another; they are aware of one another. This awareness is
what distinguishes the Relational Manifestation from the Structural Determination: the laws
of the Structural Determination are not aware of themselves; the meanings of the Relational
Manifestation are.

These three rules are not separate; they are three aspects of a single structural constraint. The
Relational Manifestation is relational because it is contextual, contextual because it is aware. The
three rules are the articulation of the category’s nature.


9.4     The Three-fold Distinction: Self-Awareness, Consciousness,
        Awareness

9.4.1    The Introduction
The Category of Relational Manifestation is the realm in which consciousness appears. But
consciousness is not a single phenomenon; it is a cluster of related phenomena. The framework
distinguishes three of them: self-awareness, consciousness (in the narrow sense), and awareness.

This distinction is introduced here but developed fully in Chapter 19. Here we give a preliminary
characterization.


9.4.2    The Preliminary Characterization
Self-awareness is the mechanism and dynamics of regulating the connection between manifes-
tations and identity. It is the activity by which a manifestation adjusts its channels of reception,
determining how much descending light it receives, how much reflective light it emits, and how
much ascending light it returns. Self-awareness operates at three levels: the Hub of Realization,
9.5. The Relation to the Hub of Signification                                                  101


the Category of Relational Manifestation, and the Category of Material Manifestation.

Consciousness (in the narrow sense) is the intensity or strength of the connection between
manifestations and identity. It is the degree to which a manifestation is connected to its identity—
the degree to which it is “lit up” by the light of identity.

Awareness is the regulation of manifestation for the reception of reflective light and intra-
category light. It is the activity by which a manifestation adjusts its channels of reception to
receive the light that is reflected from other manifestations and the light that is present within
its own category.

The three concepts are related but distinct. Self-awareness is the mechanism; consciousness is
the intensity; awareness is the regulation. Self-awareness is the most general; consciousness is a
dimension of self-awareness; awareness is a specific activity of self-awareness.




9.4.3    The Analogy of the Production Manager

A preliminary analogy may help. Self-awareness is like a production manager, who in every
moment adjusts the BOM (bill of materials) of the production process. Consciousness is the
intensity of the production—the degree to which the production is running at full capacity.
Awareness is the activity of adjusting the input channels—the activity of selecting what to
receive and what to ignore.

The full development of this analogy, and of the three-fold distinction, is given in Chapter 19.




9.5     The Relation to the Hub of Signification

The Category of Relational Manifestation is a manifestation of the Category of Structural Deter-
mination, mediated by the Hub of Signification (Chapter 8). It is the second level of refraction:
the general light of the Structural Determination is refracted by the Hub into the relational
meanings of the Relational Manifestation.

This refraction is not a loss; it is a contextualization. The Category of Structural Determination
is general multiplicity; the Category of Relational Manifestation is relational multiplicity. The
general becomes contextual, but the contextual is still general in its own way: it is the general
form of relationality, not the particular content of a specific context.

The relation between the Structural Determination and the Relational Manifestation can be
understood by analogy. Consider a word. The word, as a structural unit, is general—it is
a pattern of letters. But when the word is used in a sentence, it becomes meaningful—it is
connected to other words, to a context, to a speaker. The meaningful word is not the structural
unit; it is the structural unit in its contextualized form. Similarly, the Relational Manifestation
is the Structural Determination in its contextualized form.
102                                       Chapter 9. The Category of Relational Manifestation


9.6    The Relation to the Hub of Realization
The Category of Relational Manifestation is the environment of the Category of Material Manifes-
tation, and is encompassed by the Category of Structural Determination. Between the Relational
Manifestation and the Material Manifestation stands the Hub of Realization (Chapter 10).

The Hub of Realization receives the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation at
its Transcendental Edge, and emits the material multiplicity of the Material Manifestation at
its Immanent Edge. The Hub’s function is to realize the meanings into matter.

The relation between the Relational Manifestation and the Hub of Realization is a relation of
transmission. The Relational Manifestation transmits its manifestation—the relational multi-
plicity of meanings—to the Hub, which then realizes it into the material multiplicity of the
Material Manifestation.

The Category of Relational Manifestation has two edges: a Transcendental Edge oriented to the
Hub of Signification (the Hub above it), and an Immanent Edge oriented to the Hub of Real-
ization (the Hub below it). It receives from the Hub of Signification through its Transcendental
Edge, and it transmits to the Hub of Realization through its Immanent Edge.


9.7    Objections and Replies
Objection 9.1. The Category of Relational Manifestation seems to be a form of idealism—it
treats meaning and consciousness as fundamental.

Reply 9.1. The Category of Relational Manifestation is not a form of idealism. Idealism treats
meaning and consciousness as the whole of reality. The framework treats them as one category
among four—a real level of reality, but not the whole of reality. The material category is
equally real; the structural category is equally real; the First Determination is equally real. The
framework is a stratified realism, not an idealism.

Objection 9.2. The three-fold distinction between self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness
is too sharp. In ordinary language, these terms are used interchangeably.

Reply 9.2. In ordinary language, the terms are used loosely. But the framework’s task is to be
precise. The three phenomena are distinct: self-awareness is the mechanism, consciousness is the
intensity, awareness is the regulation. They are related but not identical. The full development
of the distinction (Chapter 19) will make this clear.

Objection 9.3. If the Relational Manifestation is the realm of consciousness, then it is the
realm of the mental. But the mental is not a separate category; it is a feature of certain material
systems (brains).

Reply 9.3. The Relational Manifestation is not a separate category from the material; it is
a level of reality that is expressed in the material. The mental is not a separate substance; it
is the reflective light within the Relational Manifestation. The material brain is the vehicle of
the mental; it is not the mental itself. This is the framework’s response to both materialism
(which reduces the mental to the material) and dualism (which treats the mental as a separate
9.8. Conclusion: The Realm of Meaning and Consciousness                                      103


substance).

Objection 9.4. The dynamism of relation seems too vague to be useful.

Reply 9.4. The dynamism of relation is not vague; it is structural. It is the unfolding of mean-
ing through the network of relations among manifestations. This unfolding has three aspects:
connection, context, and awareness. These three aspects are precise and can be operationalized
(as will be shown in the science of viability).


9.8      Conclusion: The Realm of Meaning and Consciousness
The Category of Relational Manifestation is the realm of meaning and consciousness. It is the
realm of awareness, relationship, and significance. In this category, multiplicity is relational—
manifestations are connected to one another through relations of meaning, value, and signifi-
cance.

We have seen that the Relational Manifestation is the realm of relational multiplicity, distin-
guished from the Structural Determination by its mode of multiplicity. We have seen that its
dynamism is the dynamism of relation—the unfolding of meaning through connection, context,
and awareness. We have seen that its rules are relationality, contextuality, and awareness. We
have seen the preliminary characterization of the three-fold distinction between self-awareness,
consciousness, and awareness. And we have seen its relations to the Hub of Signification and
the Hub of Realization.

The next chapter will develop the Hub of Realization—the mediating structure between the
Relational Manifestation and the Material Manifestation.
