14.1        Introduction: The Intersubjective Dimension of Expression
In the preceding chapters, we developed the Theory of Expression (Chapter 12) and the nature
of Light (Chapter 13). We saw that identity expresses itself through descent, multiplication,
and creation; that Light is the medium of this expression; and that reflection is the essence of
Light—the feature that makes expression legible.

But we did not yet explain the intersubjective dimension of expression. Why do identities express
themselves to each other ? Why do they seek to be reflected in the expressions of other identities?
And why is the unknownness of same-category identities a condition of reflection, not a defect?

This chapter answers these questions through two theorems: the Desire to Find and Unknown-
ness. These theorems are consequences of the Theory of Expression and the Axiom of Reflection.
They explain why identities seek to find themselves in the expressions of other identities, and
why the unknownness of same-category identities is a condition of reflection, not a defect.

The chapter has five parts. First, it proves the theorem of the Desire to Find. Second, it proves
the theorem of Unknownness. Third, it develops the two directions of the desire to find: vertical
and horizontal. Fourth, it shows how the desire to find applies to spatial identity (foreshadowing
Chapter 30). Fifth, it addresses objections.
14.2. The Theorem of the Desire to Find                                                            157


14.2        The Theorem of the Desire to Find

Theorem 14.1 (The Desire to Find). (T) The desire to find is the structural combination of
the necessity of expression (Axiom 0.19), the conduit of light (Axiom 0.5), and the reflective
nature of light (Axiom 0.20). It is not a contingent psychological fact but a structural feature of
identity: every identity, by its nature, desires to find itself reflected in the expression of another
identity.



Proof. By Axiom 0.19, every identity expresses itself. By Axiom 0.5, expression occurs through
light. By Axiom 0.20, light reflects by its essence. Therefore, the expression of an identity is
reflected by light. The reflection of expression is the confirmation of expression: when an identity
sees its expression reflected, it sees itself confirmed. Seeing oneself confirmed in reflection is
finding. Therefore, the desire to find is the structure of the unity of expression and reflection.
It is not an additional commitment; it is a consequence of the three axioms.



14.2.1      The Meaning of the Theorem

The theorem makes three claims.

First, the desire to find is structural, not psychological. It is not a contingent fact about
human psychology; it is a structural feature of every identity. Every identity, by its nature,
desires to find itself reflected in the expression of another identity.

Second, the desire to find is a consequence of the three axioms. It is not an additional
commitment; it follows from the necessity of expression (Axiom 0.19), the conduit of light (Axiom
0.5), and the reflective nature of light (Axiom 0.20).

Third, the desire to find is the structure of the unity of expression and reflection.
It is the desire of an identity to see itself reflected in the expression of another identity. This
reflection is the confirmation of the identity—the identity sees itself in the mirror of the other’s
expression.



14.2.2      The Implication: Descent Is Necessary for Finding

The desire to find has an important implication: descent is necessary for finding. If same-
category identities could find each other directly, there would be no need for descent. But
they cannot; they can only find each other through expression, and expression requires descent.
Therefore, the descent of categories is the condition of possibility of intersubjective finding.

This is why the categories have descent (Chapter 4). The descent is not an arbitrary feature of
the architecture; it is the condition of possibility of the desire to find. Without descent, identities
could not express themselves; without expression, they could not find each other; without finding,
the desire to find would be frustrated.
158                                            Chapter 14. The Desire to Find and Unknownness


14.3      The Theorem of Unknownness
Theorem 14.2 (Unknownness as Condition of Reflection). (T) The unknownness of same-
category identities is the condition of possibility of reflection, not a defect. If the other were
directly known, there would be no mirror; there would be no reflection. Unknownness is the
condition of individuation, and individuation is the condition of love.


Proof. If the other were directly known, there would be no need for expression; expression
would be superfluous. But expression is necessary (Axiom 0.19). Therefore, the other must be
unknown, so that expression is necessary. And because expression is reflective (Axiom 0.20), the
unknownness of the other is what makes reflection possible.


14.3.1    The Meaning of the Theorem

The theorem makes three claims.

First, unknownness is not a defect. It is not a lack of knowledge that could be overcome;
it is a structural condition of the possibility of reflection.

Second, unknownness is the condition of reflection. If the other were directly known,
there would be no mirror; there would be no reflection. The unknownness of the other is what
makes the other a mirror —a surface on which the identity can see itself reflected.

Third, unknownness is the condition of individuation and love. If same-category iden-
tities were directly known to each other, they would not be distinct identities; they would be
one identity. The unknownness is what makes them plural. And plurality is the condition of
love—for love requires an other.


14.3.2    The Implication: Love Requires an Other

The theorem has an important implication: love requires an other. If the other were directly
known, there would be no love—because love is the finding of oneself in the other, and this
finding requires that the other be unknown.

This is why the framework can say that love is not a fusion but a relation. In love, the iden-
tity does not merge with the other; it finds itself in the other, while remaining distinct. The
unknownness of the other is what makes this possible—it is the space in which love can occur.


14.4      The Two Directions of the Desire to Find
The desire to find has two directions: vertical and horizontal.


14.4.1    Vertical Desire: The Desire to Find the Source

Vertical desire is the desire to find the source—the higher category from which the identity
descends. It is the desire of the manifestation to return to its identity. It is the deepest form of
14.5. The Desire to Find in Spatial Identity                                                       159


desire—the desire of the creature for the creator, the desire of the student for the teacher, the
desire of the child for the parent.

Vertical desire is the desire for the source. It is the attraction of the manifestation to its origin.
It is the force that draws all things back to their source—the force that the framework calls
ascending light.



14.4.2    Horizontal Desire: The Desire to Find Another Identity

Horizontal desire is the desire to find another identity in the same category. It is the desire to
see oneself reflected in the expression of another identity—the desire to find oneself in the other.

Horizontal desire is the desire for the other. It is the attraction of an identity to another
identity, mediated by their expressions. It is the force that grounds community, friendship, and
solidarity—the force that the framework calls horizontal love.



14.4.3    The Unity of Vertical and Horizontal Desire

Vertical and horizontal desire are not two separate forces; they are two directions of a single
force. Both are ascending light; both are the attraction of manifestation to its source; both are
the desire to find.

The difference is only in the direction: vertical desire is directed toward the source; horizontal
desire is directed toward the other. But both are expressions of the same fundamental structure—
the desire of an identity to find itself reflected in the expression of another identity.

This unity is why the framework can say that love is the foundation of ethics (Chapter 25).
Ethics is not merely the pursuit of the good; it is the pursuit of the good through the finding of
oneself in the other. And this finding is the fulfillment of the desire to find—the desire that is
the structural feature of every identity.




14.5      The Desire to Find in Spatial Identity

14.5.1    The Extension to Places

The desire to find is not limited to personal identity. It extends to spatial identity as well. Just
as identities desire to find themselves reflected in other identities, places desire to find themselves
reflected in other places.

This is a consequence of the same structure that grounds the desire to find in general. A place is
an expression of an invariant structure—its genealogical identity (Chapter 30). This expression is
reflected by other places—their boundaries, their divisions, their shared geological and ecological
lineages. The reflection of a place’s expression by other places is the confirmation of the place’s
expression—it is the place’s finding of itself.
160                                          Chapter 14. The Desire to Find and Unknownness


14.5.2     The Legibility of Places
Two neighboring provinces are unknown to each other directly; they find each other through their
expressions—their boundaries, their divisions, their shared geological and ecological lineages.
The desire to find is not merely a feature of personal identity; it is a feature of spatial identity
as well.

This is why places with rich genealogies—places that have expressed themselves in many ways—
are more “legible” to other places: they have more to reflect, and therefore more to find. A place
with a rich history, a rich ecology, a rich culture, is a place that has expressed itself in many
ways; it has many mirrors in which other places can find themselves.

14.5.3     The Ethics of Place
This has an important consequence for the ethics of place. If a place’s expression is distorted—if
its genealogy is interrupted, if its boundaries are arbitrarily redrawn, if its ecological and human
lineages are severed—then its capacity to find itself in other places is diminished. The place be-
comes “illegible”—it loses its capacity to be recognized as the same place across transformations.

The preservation of a place’s genealogy is therefore not merely a matter of historical interest;
it is a matter of the place’s viability—its capacity to continue expressing itself, and to continue
finding itself in the expressions of other places. This will be developed in Chapter 30.


14.6       Objections and Replies
Objection 14.1. The desire to find is a psychological concept, not a metaphysical one.

Reply 14.1. The desire to find is not a psychological concept; it is a structural feature of
identity (Theorem 14.1). It follows from the necessity of expression (Axiom 0.19), the conduit
of light (Axiom 0.5), and the reflective nature of light (Axiom 0.20). It is as structural as the
laws of physics.

Objection 14.2. If same-category identities are unknown to each other, then love is impossible.

Reply 14.2. This objection confuses unknownness with isolation. Same-category identities
are unknown directly, but they can find each other through expression. Love is precisely this
finding—it is the attraction of an identity to another identity, mediated by their expressions.
The unknownness is not a barrier to love; it is the condition of love (Theorem 14.2).

Objection 14.3. The desire to find is just a restatement of the concept of love.

Reply 14.3. The desire to find is not a restatement of love; it is the structure of love. Love is
the fulfillment of the desire to find—the finding of oneself in the other. The desire to find is the
orientation; love is the fulfillment. They are related but distinct.

Objection 14.4. The two directions of the desire to find—vertical and horizontal—are arbitrary.
Why not have more directions?

Reply 14.4. The two directions are not arbitrary; they correspond to the two fundamental
orientations of an identity. Vertical desire is oriented toward the source—the higher category
14.7. Conditions of Revision and Falsification                                                           161


from which the identity descends. Horizontal desire is oriented toward the other—the same-
category identity in which the identity seeks to find itself. These are the two fundamental
orientations because they correspond to the two fundamental relations of an identity: its relation
to its source and its relation to its peers.

Objection 14.5. The extension of the desire to find to spatial identity is a mere analogy. Places
do not really desire anything.

Reply 14.5. The extension is not a mere analogy; it is a structural extension. The desire to find
is a structural feature of every identity—whether personal or spatial. A place is an expression
of an invariant structure (its genealogical identity); this expression is reflected by other places;
the reflection is the place’s finding of itself. The framework does not claim that places have
psychological desires; it claims that they have structural desires—the same desire that every
identity has, to find itself reflected in the expression of another.

Objection 14.6. If the desire to find is structural, then it cannot be frustrated. But we know
that identities often fail to find themselves in the expressions of others.

Reply 14.6. The desire to find is structural, but its fulfillment is not guaranteed. The desire
is the orientation; the fulfillment depends on the conditions—on whether the other’s expression
adequately reflects the identity. When the reflection is distorted (sediment), the desire is frus-
trated. This is why sediment is an existential burden (Chapter 21)—it is the accumulation of
frustrated finding.


14.7      Conditions of Revision and Falsification

    Conditions of Revision and Falsification.         What would count against the claims of
    this chapter.

     • Against the (T) Theorem of the Desire to Find: a demonstration that one of the three axioms
       it invokes (0.19, 0.5, 0.20) is false or inapplicable, or that the inference from the axioms to
       the theorem is invalid.

     • Against the (T) Theorem of Unknownness: a demonstration that direct knowledge of the
       other is compatible with expression (i.e., that expression would not be superfluous even if
       the other were directly known).

     • Against the (A) distinction between vertical and horizontal desire: a demonstration that
       there are additional fundamental orientations of identity, or that the two can be reduced to
       one.

     • Against the (A) extension to spatial identity: a demonstration that places are not expressions
       of invariant structures, or that their expressions are not reflected by other places.




14.8      Conclusion: The Intersubjective Dimension of Expression
The theorems of the Desire to Find and Unknownness complete the development of the medium
of expression. They show that expression is not a solitary process—it is an intersubjective
162                                         Chapter 14. The Desire to Find and Unknownness


process. Identities express themselves in order to find themselves in the expressions of other
identities; and the unknownness of the other is the condition of this finding.

We have seen that the desire to find is a structural feature of every identity—not a contingent
psychological fact. We have seen that the unknownness of same-category identities is the condi-
tion of reflection, not a defect. We have seen that the desire to find has two directions—vertical
and horizontal—and that both are expressions of a single force. And we have seen that the
desire to find extends to spatial identity—places, like persons, desire to find themselves in the
expressions of other places.

The next chapter will develop Category-Relative Predication—the principle that resolves the
apparent tension between the rigidity of identity and the dynamism of expression. It will show
that rigidity and dynamism are not absolute predicates, but are defined relative to a category.

15.1      Introduction: The Apparent Tension
In the preceding chapters, we have developed the Theory of Expression (Chapter 12), the nature
of Light (Chapter 13), and the theorems of the Desire to Find and Unknownness (Chapter 14).
We have seen that identity expresses itself through descent, multiplication, and creation—it
descends from the higher categories to the lower, it multiplies in the lower categories, and it
creates new manifestations at each level.

But this raises an apparent tension. On the one hand, we have said that identity is rigid —it
is invariant under all transformations of its manifestations (Axiom 0.3). On the other hand,
we have said that identity is dynamic—it is in a state of expression, continuously descending,
multiplying, and creating. How can identity be both rigid and dynamic?

A critic might say: this is a contradiction. Rigidity and dynamism are incompatible. The
framework is incoherent.

This chapter argues that there is no contradiction. The apparent tension is resolved by Category-
164                                                     Chapter 15. Category-Relative Predication


Relative Predication—the principle that metaphysical predicates are not absolute but are defined
relative to a category. Identity is rigid with respect to its manifestations, but dynamic with respect
to the higher category of which it is itself a manifestation. This is not a contradiction; it is a
structural feature of the four-category architecture.

The chapter has six parts. First, it states the Axiom of Identity Rigidity and defends it. Second,
it states the Axiom of Category-Relative Predication and explains its role. Third, it resolves
the apparent tension between rigidity and dynamism. Fourth, it develops the Schrödinger’s cat
analogy. Fifth, it distinguishes the framework’s resolution from decoherence. Sixth, it explores
the consequences of Category-Relative Predication for persistence, moral responsibility, and the
integrity of the self.


15.2        The Axiom of Identity Rigidity
Axiom 0.3 (Identity Rigidity), Reinterpreted. (A)Identity is invariant under all transfor-
mations of its manifestations. It is rigid: it does not bend, it does not compromise, it does not
admit of degrees. This rigidity is defined with respect to the manifestations of the identity, not
with respect to the higher category of which the identity is itself a manifestation.


15.2.1      The Argument from Logical Necessity
Why must identity be rigid with respect to its manifestations? The answer is a matter of
logical necessity. Suppose that identity could be “more or less” present—that an entity could be
“partially” itself, or “gradually” lose its identity over time. What would this mean?

It would mean that there is a continuum of similarity, along which entities can be placed accord-
ing to how “close” they are to being the same. But a continuum of similarity is not identity. It
is the absence of identity.

If we allow identity to be a matter of degree, we lose the very concept of identity. We are left
with a spectrum of resemblance, but no principled way to distinguish “the same” from “merely
similar.”

Consider an example. Suppose we say that a person is “70% herself” after a traumatic experience.
What does this mean? Does it mean that 30% of her identity has been lost? If so, what exactly
has been lost? The concept of a “partial identity” is unintelligible because identity is not a
quantity that can be divided. Either a person is the same person, or she is not. There is no
middle ground.

This is not a stipulation; it is a consequence of the concept of identity. Identity is the condi-
tion of persistence. If persistence could be partial, then the concept of persistence would be
unintelligible.


15.2.2      The Contrast with Properties
It is important to distinguish the rigidity of identity from the degrees of properties. Properties
can admit of degrees: a room can be “more or less” warm, a person can be “more or less” tall,
15.3. The Axiom of Category-Relative Predication                                                 165


a solution can be “more or less” acidic. But identity is not a property—it is the condition of
persistence itself. And as such, it cannot admit of degrees.

This distinction is crucial. Many philosophers have been misled by the fact that we speak of
“degrees of identity” in ordinary language. We say that someone is “not themselves today,” or
that a building is “no longer the same.” But these are loose ways of speaking. Strictly speaking,
either the person is the same person, or they are not. The apparent degrees are degrees of
manifestation, not degrees of identity.


15.3     The Axiom of Category-Relative Predication
Axiom 0.21 (Category-Relative Predication). (A)Metaphysical predicates—such as rigid-
ity, dynamism, unity, multiplicity, temporality, atemporality—are not absolute. They are defined
relative to a category. An identity is rigid with respect to its manifestations, but dynamic with
respect to the higher category of which it is itself a manifestation. This is not a contradiction;
it is a structural feature of the four-category architecture. The principle resolves the apparent
tension between identity rigidity (Axiom 0.3) and the fact that every identity is itself a manifes-
tation of a higher identity: rigidity and dynamism are not absolute predicates but are defined
relative to the category from which they are predicated.


15.3.1    The Meaning of the Axiom
The axiom makes three claims.

First, metaphysical predicates are not absolute. Predicates like rigidity, dynamism, unity,
multiplicity, temporality, and atemporality are not properties that a thing has simpliciter. They
are properties that a thing has relative to a category.

Second, the same thing can have different predicates relative to different categories.
An identity can be rigid with respect to its manifestations (in one category) and dynamic with
respect to the higher category (in another category). This is not a contradiction; it is a structural
feature of the four-category architecture.

Third, the category from which a predicate is predicated is determined by the
position of the thing in the architecture. The identity is located in a particular category;
the manifestations are located in lower categories; the higher category is located above. The
predicates are defined relative to these positions.


15.3.2    The Structural Analogy
The axiom has a structural analogy in quantum mechanics. In quantum mechanics, the proper-
ties of a system—such as position, momentum, spin—are not absolute; they are defined relative
to a measurement basis. The same system can have different properties relative to different
measurement bases. This is not a contradiction; it is a structural feature of quantum mechanics.

Similarly, in the philosophy of viability, the properties of an identity—such as rigidity,
dynamism—are not absolute; they are defined relative to a category. The same identity can
166                                                     Chapter 15. Category-Relative Predication


have different properties relative to different categories. This is not a contradiction; it is a
structural feature of the four-category architecture.

The analogy is not perfect—the measurement basis in quantum mechanics is a chosen basis, while
the category in the philosophy of viability is a structural position. But the analogy captures the
essential point: predicates are not absolute, but relative to a frame of reference.


15.4      Resolving the Apparent Tension

15.4.1     The Apparent Tension Restated
The apparent tension is this: identity is said to be rigid (Axiom 0.3) and dynamic (Theory of
Expression, Chapter 12). How can it be both?


15.4.2     The Resolution
The resolution is given by Category-Relative Predication. Rigidity and dynamism are not abso-
lute predicates; they are defined relative to a category.

Rigidity with respect to manifestations: The identity does not change under transforma-
tions of its manifestations. It is the same identity through all its manifestations. This is the
rigidity of identity.

Dynamism with respect to the higher category: The identity is itself a manifestation of
a higher identity, and therefore is in a state of expression. It is dynamic as a manifestation, not
as an identity.

These two are not contradictory; they are two descriptions of the same identity, from two different
categorical perspectives. The identity is rigid as an identity (with respect to its manifestations)
and dynamic as a manifestation (with respect to its higher category). It is the same structural
state, seen from two different angles.


15.4.3     The Mechanism of Resolution
In physics, the superposition is resolved by decoherence or measurement. In the framework,
the apparent contradiction between rigidity and dynamism is resolved by categorical position.
The observer does not choose the category; the observer is situated in a category. This is not
relativism, because the categorical position is structural, not arbitrary.

The distinction between context and perspective, introduced in Chapter 3 (§3.3), is crucial here.
A context is a structural position in the architecture; a perspective is the observer’s vantage
point within a context. The observer does not choose the context; the observer is situated in
it. The context determines which predicates are applicable; the perspective determines how the
observer apprehends them.

The observer who is situated in the category of the identity sees the identity as rigid—because
from that position, the manifestations are the variable appearances, and the identity is the
invariant structure. The observer who is situated in the higher category sees the identity as
15.5. The Schrödinger’s Cat Analogy                                                            167


dynamic—because from that position, the identity is itself a manifestation, and it is in a state
of expression.

Both observers are correct, but they are describing the same structure from different perspectives.
This is not a contradiction; it is a perspectival description of a stratified reality.


15.5      The Schrödinger’s Cat Analogy

15.5.1    The Analogy
Consider the famous thought experiment of Schrödinger’s cat. The cat is in a superposition of
“alive” and “dead.” Is this a contradiction? No—because “alive” and “dead” are not absolute
predicates; they are defined relative to a measurement basis. The superposition is a single state,
not two contradictory states.

Similarly, an identity is rigid with respect to its manifestations and dynamic with respect to its
higher category. This is not a contradiction; it is a single structural state, described from two
different categorical perspectives.

15.5.2    The Limits of the Analogy
The analogy has limits. In quantum mechanics, the superposition is a physical state—it can be
measured, manipulated, and eventually decohered. In the philosophy of viability, the “superpo-
sition” of rigidity and dynamism is not a physical state; it is a structural state—a description of
the same identity from two different categorical positions.

But the analogy captures the essential point: an apparent contradiction can be resolved by
recognizing that the predicates are not absolute but are defined relative to a frame of reference.
In quantum mechanics, the frame of reference is the measurement basis; in the philosophy of
viability, the frame of reference is the category.

15.5.3    The Pedagogical Value of the Analogy
The analogy has pedagogical value. It helps the reader to see that apparent contradictions can
be resolved by distinguishing the frames of reference. This is the essence of Category-Relative
Predication: the predicates are not absolute, but are defined relative to a category. Once the
category is specified, the apparent contradiction dissolves.


15.6      The Difference from Decoherence

15.6.1    The Question
The Schrödinger’s cat analogy raises an important question. In physics, the superposition is
resolved by decoherence—a physical process by which the superposition is reduced to a definite
state through interaction with the environment. In the framework, the apparent contradiction
between rigidity and dynamism is resolved by categorical position. Are these two mechanisms
equivalent? If not, does the difference lead to relativism?
168                                                    Chapter 15. Category-Relative Predication


15.6.2    The Answer: Structural vs. Physical

The two mechanisms are not equivalent. Decoherence is a physical process—it occurs indepen-
dently of any observer, through the interaction of the system with its environment. Categorical
position is a structural position—it is the position of the observer in the architecture of reality.

The difference is crucial. In physics, the resolution of the superposition is independent of the
observer —decoherence is a physical process that occurs whether or not anyone observes it. In the
framework, the resolution is dependent on the categorical position of the observer —the observer’s
position in the architecture determines which predicates are applicable.


15.6.3    The Response to Relativism

The dependence on the observer’s position might seem to lead to relativism. But it does not,
because the categorical position is structural, not arbitrary. The observer does not choose the
category; the observer is situated in it. The category is determined by the structure of the
identity and its manifestation.

The observer cannot “choose any category”; they are situated in a category that is determined
by the structure of the identity and its manifestation. This is not relativism; it is a recognition
of the structural nature of the observer’s position.


15.6.4    The Consequence

The consequence is that the framework’s resolution of the apparent contradiction is structural,
not physical. It does not require a physical process of decoherence; it requires a structural
recognition of the observer’s categorical position. This is what distinguishes the framework’s
resolution from the physical resolution of the quantum superposition.


15.7     Consequences of Category-Relative Predication
Category-Relative Predication has several consequences for the framework.


15.7.1    Persistence Through Time

The first consequence is the possibility of persistence through time. If identity were a matter
of degree, we could not say that an entity persists through change; we could only say that it
“gradually becomes” something else. But with Category-Relative Predication, we can say that
the entity remains the same through all its transformations.

This consequence is profound. It means that change is intelligible as the change of a single entity,
rather than as a sequence of unrelated states. It means that memory, history, and narrative are
possible. It means that we can speak of an entity’s life as a unified whole, rather than as a
disconnected series of moments.

Persistence through time is persistence through the three modes of light. Descending light
flows continuously from identity to manifestation. Ascending light flows continuously from
15.8. The Categories and the Predicates                                                          169


manifestation to identity. Reflective light flows continuously within each category. The identity
is conserved because the light is conserved.


15.7.2    Moral Responsibility

The second consequence is the possibility of moral responsibility. If identity were a matter of
degree, we could not hold persons responsible for their past actions. But with Category-Relative
Predication, we can say that the person who acted yesterday is the same person who is held
responsible today.

This consequence is central to ethics. Without rigidity, the concept of moral responsibility would
collapse. If a person could be “partially” themselves, then they could be “partially” responsible for
their actions—a conclusion that is unintelligible. Moral responsibility requires that the person
who acted and the person who is held responsible are the same person, not merely similar.


15.7.3    The Integrity of the Self

The third consequence is the integrity of the self. If identity were a matter of degree, the self
would be a fragile, shifting thing. But with Category-Relative Predication, the self is a stable,
unified thing—the same self through all its transformations.

This consequence is important for psychology and psychiatry. Many psychological disorders—
such as dissociative identity disorder—involve a fragmentation of the self. The Axiom of Identity
Rigidity does not deny that such fragmentation occurs; it locates it at the level of manifestation.
The self may appear fragmented, but its identity is conserved. The task of therapy is not to
restore a lost identity, but to reconstruct a coherent pseudo-identity that is adequate to the
invariant identity.


15.7.4    The Constancy of the Light

The fourth consequence is the constancy of the light. The Axiom of Identity Rigidity has a
profound implication for the Light of Identity: the light is constant. It does not diminish or
increase. It does not bend or compromise. It is the same light that flows from the same identity,
regardless of the manifestations it generates.

This constancy is the source of the identity’s invariance. If the light could change, the identity
could change. But the light cannot change, because it is the light of the identity—it is the
identity’s own self-expression. The constancy of the light is the rigidity of the identity.



15.8     The Categories and the Predicates

Category-Relative Predication applies to all the categories. Each category has its own char-
acteristic predicates, and the same identity can have different predicates relative to different
categories.
170                                                    Chapter 15. Category-Relative Predication


15.8.1    The First Determination
In the Category of First Determination, identity is absolutely rigid. It is pure unity, pure
invariance, pure light. There is no change, no multiplicity, no time. The predicates of the First
Determination are unity, invariance, and atemporality.

15.8.2    The Structural Determination
In the Category of Structural Determination, identity is relatively rigid. It is specified into the
class of allowable transformations. The predicates of the Structural Determination are generality,
lawfulness, and necessity.

15.8.3    The Relational Manifestation
In the Category of Relational Manifestation, identity is relatively dynamic. It is expressed
through relations of meaning and consciousness. The predicates of the Relational Manifestation
are relationality, contextuality, and consciousness.

15.8.4    The Material Manifestation
In the Category of Material Manifestation, identity is most dynamic. It is expressed through
material forms. The predicates of the Material Manifestation are materiality, discreteness, and
transience.

15.8.5    The Relativity of the Predicates
The same identity can be described as rigid in one category and dynamic in another. This is
not a contradiction; it is a consequence of the stratified nature of reality. The identity is one,
but its predicates are many—because the categories are many.


15.9     Objections and Replies
Objection 15.1. Category-Relative Predication makes the framework relativistic. If predicates
are relative to a category, then anything goes.

Reply 15.1. Category-Relative Predication is not relativism. The category in which an observer
is situated is not a matter of choice; it is a structural position. The observer does not choose the
category; the observer is situated in it. This is not relativism; it is a recognition of the structure
of the observer’s position.

Objection 15.2. The distinction between rigidity and dynamism is just a verbal trick. The
framework is still incoherent.

Reply 15.2. The distinction is not a verbal trick; it is a structural distinction. Rigidity and
dynamism are not absolute predicates; they are defined relative to a category. This is not a
linguistic stipulation; it is a consequence of the stratified nature of reality. The same identity
can be rigid in one category and dynamic in another—just as the same object can be at rest in
one frame of reference and in motion in another.
15.9. Objections and Replies                                                                     171


Objection 15.3. If identity is dynamic with respect to the higher category, then it is not really
rigid. The rigidity is an illusion.

Reply 15.3. The rigidity is not an illusion; it is a relative rigidity. The identity is rigid with
respect to its manifestations—it does not change under transformations of its manifestations. It
is dynamic with respect to the higher category—it is itself a manifestation of a higher identity.
Both are real; both are structural features of the identity. The rigidity is not an illusion; it is a
perspectival description of a stratified reality.

Objection 15.4. The Schrödinger’s cat analogy is misleading. In quantum mechanics, the
superposition is a physical state; in the framework, the “superposition” of rigidity and dynamism
is not a physical state.

Reply 15.4. The analogy is not perfect, but it is instructive. It helps the reader to see that
apparent contradictions can be resolved by recognizing that predicates are not absolute but are
defined relative to a frame of reference. In quantum mechanics, the frame of reference is the
measurement basis; in the framework, the frame of reference is the category. The analogy does
not claim that the framework is a form of quantum mechanics; it claims that the structure of
the resolution is analogous.

Objection 15.5. The difference from decoherence seems to introduce observer-dependence into
the framework. This is a form of idealism.

Reply 15.5. The difference from decoherence does not introduce observer-dependence in the
idealist sense. The observer’s categorical position is structural, not arbitrary. The observer
does not create the category; the observer is situated in it. The category is determined by the
structure of the identity and its manifestation, not by the observer’s choice. This is not idealism;
it is a structural realism about the observer’s position.

Objection 15.6. Category-Relative Predication is a form of relativism about truth. It denies
that there is an absolute truth.

Reply 15.6. Category-Relative Predication is not relativism about truth. It does not deny
that there is an absolute truth; it denies that the truth can be captured by absolute predicates.
The truth about an identity is always relative to a category—but this does not mean that it is
arbitrary. The category is a structural position, not a subjective choice. The truth about an
identity is objective—it is determined by the structure of the identity and the structure of the
category—but it is not absolute in the sense of being independent of all categories.

Objection 15.7. If Category-Relative Predication is true, then we can never say what an
identity really is. We can only say what it is relative to a category.

Reply 15.7. This is correct, and it is a consequence of the Principle of Inherent Observer
Incompleteness (Axiom 0.6). We can never say what an identity really is, because we can never
access the identity independently of a category. But this does not mean that we can say nothing;
it means that what we say is always relative to a category—and that this relativity is not a defect,
but a feature of the structure of reality.

      Conditions of Revision and Falsification.           What would count against the claims of

      • Against the (T) argument from logical necessity for Identity Rigidity: a coherent account of

      • Against the (A) Category-Relative Predication: a demonstration that apparent contradic-

      • Against the (T) distinction from decoherence: a demonstration that the framework’s resolu-

15.11        Conclusion: The Resolution of the Tension

Category-Relative Predication resolves the apparent tension between rigidity and dynamism.
Identity is rigid with respect to its manifestations, but dynamic with respect to the higher
category. This is not a contradiction; it is a structural feature of the four-category architecture.

We have seen that rigidity and dynamism are not absolute predicates, but are defined relative to
a category. We have seen that the same identity can be described as rigid in one category and
dynamic in another, without contradiction. We have seen that this resolution has important
consequences for persistence, moral responsibility, the integrity of the self, and the constancy
of the light. We have seen that the Schrödinger’s cat analogy illuminates the structure of the
resolution. And we have seen that the framework’s resolution differs from decoherence in being
structural rather than physical.

This completes Part IV: The Dynamic Engine. We have developed the Theory of Expression
(Chapter 12), the nature of Light (Chapter 13), the theorems of the Desire to Find and Un-
knownness (Chapter 14), and Category-Relative Predication (this chapter). These four chapters
are the dynamic engine that animates the static architecture established in Part III.

The next part (Part V: Relational Rules and Epistemology) will develop the relational rules
and the epistemology of the observer: Identity Rigidity, Conservation, and Non-Duplicability;
Pure Relationality; Inherent Observer Incompleteness; the Three-fold Distinction between Self-
Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness; and Multi-Layered Logic.

The horizon is open. The conversation continues.

Part V: A Note on the Status of the Re-
lational Rules

Part V develops the relational rules that govern the connections between identities and the epis-
temology of the observer. Its central claims—Identity Rigidity, Conservation, Non-Duplicability,
Pure Relationality, Inherent Observer Incompleteness, the Three-fold Distinction between Self-
Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness, and Multi-Layered Logic—are the framework’s most
directly criticizable claims, because they concern the relation between the framework and the
observer who assesses it.

Three cautions are in order before we begin.

First, the transcendental argument for Identity Conservation (Chapter 16) is (T),
and its conclusion is (A). The argument shows that conservation is a condition of possibility
of finite inquiry into identity; the reception of conservation as an axiom is a commitment. The
reader who accepts the argument but hesitates to receive it as an axiom is not refuted; they are
simply operating within a different framework.

Second, the three-fold distinction (Chapter 19) is (A), but its elements vary in
status. The claim that self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness are distinct is (A); the
specific characterizations (mechanism, intensity, regulation) are (A); the BOM analogy is a
heuristic, not a metaphysical claim. The reader who accepts the distinction but rejects the
specific characterizations is invited to propose alternatives.

Third, Multi-Layered Logic (Chapter 20) is (A), and the practical test of §20.4 is
offered as a (T) operationalization, not as a proof. The logic is offered as the framework’s
most ambitious attempt to resolve the classical paradoxes; the practical test is offered as the
framework’s way of disciplining its own use. A reader who accepts the logic but finds the test
insufficient is invited to propose a better test—the framework’s claim is that some such test is
necessary, not that this particular test is final.

Each chapter in Part V opens with a status box. The reader is invited to consult it before
engaging with the chapter’s argument.

The horizon is open. The conversation continues.

Keywords: Identity Rigidity, Identity Conservation, Non-Duplicability, Identity of Indis-

16.1     Introduction: Three Structural Properties
In the preceding chapters, we have developed the Theory of Expression (Chapter 12), the nature
of Light (Chapter 13), the theorems of the Desire to Find and Unknownness (Chapter 14), and
Category-Relative Predication (Chapter 15). We have seen that identity expresses itself through
descent, multiplication, and creation; that Light is the medium of this expression; and that
rigidity and dynamism are not absolute predicates but are defined relative to a category.

But we have not yet developed three structural properties that are implicit in these chapters and
that are essential to the framework: rigidity, conservation, and non-duplicability. This chapter
develops them.

The three properties are closely related. Rigidity is the invariant structure of identity under the
transformations of its manifestations. Conservation is the persistence of this invariant structure
across time. Non-duplicability is the impossibility of copying this invariant structure. Together,
178                          Chapter 16. Identity Rigidity, Conservation, and Non-Duplicability


they constitute the structural core of the framework’s account of identity.

The chapter has five parts. First, it develops the Axiom of Identity Rigidity (already introduced
in Chapter 15, but here developed in full). Second, it develops the Axiom of Identity Conser-
vation. Third, it develops the Axiom of Non-Duplicability. Fourth, it addresses the classical
puzzles of personal identity (Locke’s memory criterion, Reid’s problem, teleportation, cloning,
fission). Fifth, it addresses objections.


16.2      Identity Rigidity
Axiom 0.3 (Identity Rigidity). (A)Identity is invariant under all transformations of its man-
ifestations. It is rigid: it does not bend, it does not compromise, it does not admit of degrees.
A structure either is invariant under the specified transformations, or it is not. This axiom is
to be read in the light of Axiom 0.21 (Category-Relative Predication): the rigidity is defined with
respect to the manifestations of the identity, not with respect to the higher category of which the
identity is itself a manifestation.


16.2.1     The Argument from Logical Necessity
The argument for the rigidity of identity is the argument from logical necessity, already sketched
in Chapter 15. The argument can be stated as follows.

Suppose that identity could be “more or less” present—that an entity could be “partially” itself,
or “gradually” lose its identity over time. What would this mean?

It would mean that there is a continuum of similarity, along which entities can be placed accord-
ing to how “close” they are to being the same. But a continuum of similarity is not identity. It
is the absence of identity. If we allow identity to be a matter of degree, we lose the very concept
of identity. We are left with a spectrum of resemblance, but no principled way to distinguish
“the same” from “merely similar.”

Consider an example. Suppose we say that a person is “70% herself” after a traumatic experience.
What does this mean? Does it mean that 30% of her identity has been lost? If so, what exactly
has been lost? The concept of a “partial identity” is unintelligible because identity is not a
quantity that can be divided. Either a person is the same person, or she is not. There is no
middle ground.

This is not a stipulation; it is a consequence of the concept of identity. Identity is the condi-
tion of persistence. If persistence could be partial, then the concept of persistence would be
unintelligible.


16.2.2     The Contrast with Properties
It is important to distinguish the rigidity of identity from the degrees of properties. Properties
can admit of degrees: a room can be “more or less” warm, a person can be “more or less” tall,
a solution can be “more or less” acidic. But identity is not a property—it is the condition of
persistence itself. And as such, it cannot admit of degrees.
16.3. Identity Conservation                                                                     179


This distinction is crucial. Many philosophers have been misled by the fact that we speak of
“degrees of identity” in ordinary language. We say that someone is “not themselves today,” or
that a building is “no longer the same.” But these are loose ways of speaking. Strictly speaking,
either the person is the same person, or they are not. The apparent degrees are degrees of
manifestation, not degrees of identity.

16.2.3    The Modal Status of Rigidity
The Axiom of Identity Rigidity is not a contingent truth about the world; it is a necessary truth
about the concept of identity. It is necessary because it follows from the very meaning of identity.
To deny it would be to use the word “identity” in a way that is inconsistent with its meaning.

But we must be careful. The necessity here is conceptual, not metaphysical. We are not claiming
that identity is rigid in all possible worlds; we are claiming that the concept of identity is rigid.
Whether there are entities that have identity in the relevant sense is a separate question. The
Axiom of Identity Rigidity is a conceptual axiom, not a metaphysical one.


16.3     Identity Conservation
Axiom 0.10 (Identity Conservation). (A)Identity is invariant under all temporal transfor-
mations of its manifestations. Manifestations may vary with time; identity itself is conserved.

16.3.1    The Argument from Temporal Invariance
If identity is rigid—if it is invariant under transformations of its manifestations—then it is
invariant under temporal transformations as well. Time is just one dimension of transformation.

This argument is simple, but it has profound consequences. It means that identity is not some-
thing that happens to persist; it is something that is conserved. Persistence is not an achieve-
ment; it is a structural feature of identity. An identity does not “struggle” to persist; it is
conserved, as long as it remains the same identity.

16.3.2    The Transcendental Grounding
The Axiom of Identity Conservation is a strong axiom. It claims that identity is invariant under
all temporal transformations, no matter how radical. This claim requires justification beyond
the appeal to rigidity.

The framework provides a transcendental argument. The argument does not derive conservation
from a descriptive premise; it shows that conservation is a condition of possibility of certain
experiences that we incontrovertibly have.

1. We have experiences of temporal continuity. We remember the past; we anticipate the future;
   we recognize objects and persons across time.

2. The possibility of temporal continuity requires that the objects and persons we recognize
   remain the same across time. If identity were not conserved, there would be no “same object”
   to recognize.
180                           Chapter 16. Identity Rigidity, Conservation, and Non-Duplicability


3. Therefore, identity conservation is a transcendental condition of the possibility of temporal
      continuity.

4. A transcendental condition cannot be coherently denied. To deny it is to undermine the very
      possibility of the experience one is describing.

This argument is transcendental in the Kantian sense: it does not derive conservation from
experience; it shows that conservation is a condition of the possibility of experience. (The
transcendental methodology is developed in Chapter 2.)

The argument has a conditional form: if we have experiences of temporal continuity, then
identity is conserved. We do have such experiences—in memory, in anticipation, in recognition,
in moral responsibility. Therefore, identity is conserved.

A critic may object that the argument only shows conservation is presupposed by our experience,
not that it holds in reality. This is correct, but it is not a refutation. The framework does not
claim to demonstrate conservation from a God’s-eye view; it claims to show that conservation
is a condition of possibility of any finite inquiry into identity. This is consistent with Axiom
0.22—the philosopher, too, is subject to the limits of finite inquiry.




16.3.3       The Three Moments of Temporal Experience

To see the force of the transcendental argument, consider the three moments of temporal expe-
rience.

First, memory. When I remember a past event, I remember it as mine. The person who
experienced the event is the same person who remembers it. Without conservation, memory
would be impossible—there would be no “I” to remember.

Second, anticipation. When I anticipate a future event, I anticipate it as something that will
happen to me. The person who will experience the event is the same person who anticipates it.
Without conservation, anticipation would be impossible.

Third, recognition. When I recognize an object or person across time, I recognize it as the
same. Without conservation, recognition would be impossible—there would be no “same” to
recognize.

These three moments are not independent; they are three aspects of a single structure of temporal
experience. And all three presuppose the conservation of identity.




16.4        Non-Duplicability of Identity

Axiom 0.9 (Non-Duplicability of Identity). (A)Identity cannot be copied.                 Pseudo-
Identities and information can be duplicated; identity cannot. Two bodies are two manifestations
of one identity, not two identities.
16.4. Non-Duplicability of Identity                                                              181


16.4.1      The Distinction Between Manifestation and Identity
The key to understanding non-duplicability is the distinction between manifestation and identity.
A manifestation is a pattern of observable properties. An identity is an invariant structure—a
pattern of relations that persists through transformations.

Manifestations can be duplicated. You can copy a painting, a song, a document. But the copy
is not the original; it is a different entity with the same pattern. The identity of the original—its
specific history, its specific relations, its specific place in the world—is not duplicated. What is
duplicated is the pattern of observable properties, not the identity that expresses itself through
them.

Consider a simple example. Suppose you have a letter written by a famous author. You can
photocopy the letter, producing a perfect reproduction of its visible content. But the photocopy
is not the original letter. The original has a history—it was written by the author’s hand, it
was sent to a specific recipient, it has been preserved for decades. The photocopy has none
of this history. The visible pattern is the same, but the expression is different: the original is
an expression of the author’s identity in the material context of handwriting and paper; the
photocopy is an expression of the photocopier’s identity in the material context of toner and
light. The visible pattern is shared, but the identities that express themselves through it are
distinct.

16.4.2      The Direct Argument for Non-Duplicability
The distinction between manifestation and identity is necessary but not sufficient. We must also
provide a direct argument for why identity cannot be duplicated.

Consider what duplication would require. If identity I were duplicated, there would be two
distinct entities, I1 and I2 , each having the same identity as I. But if I1 and I2 are distinct,
they must differ in some respect—otherwise they would not be distinct. And if they differ in
some respect, then at least one of them differs from I in that respect. But then that one is not
the same as I—contradiction.

Therefore, identity cannot be duplicated. Any apparent duplication is a duplication of manifes-
tation, not of identity.

16.4.3      The Metaphysical Presupposition: Identity of Indiscernibles
The direct argument for non-duplicability presupposes the Principle of Identity of Indiscernibles:
if two entities are identical in all respects, they are the same entity. This principle is not
universally accepted; some philosophers accept it, others reject it.

The framework adopts the Principle of Identity of Indiscernibles as a working assumption (A). It
does not claim to prove it; it claims that it is the most plausible account of the relation between
identity and difference. If a critic rejects the principle, the direct argument for non-duplicability
does not go through—but neither does the possibility of genuine duplication. The choice is
between accepting the principle and accepting that identity can be duplicated. The framework
chooses the former.
182                         Chapter 16. Identity Rigidity, Conservation, and Non-Duplicability


This does not mean that the principle is an axiom of the framework. It is a presupposition of
the argument for non-duplicability. A critic who rejects the principle can still accept the rest
of the framework; they simply cannot use the direct argument for non-duplicability. This is a
consequence of the fallibilist epistemology we adopted in Chapter 2—and of the extension of
that epistemology to the philosopher in Axiom 0.22.



16.4.4       The Distinction Between Numerical and Qualitative Difference

A critic may object that two entities can differ numerically without differing qualitatively. On
this view, I1 and I2 could be qualitatively identical (having all the same properties) while being
numerically distinct (being two different entities). If so, identity could be duplicated.

Our response is that numerical difference is itself a qualitative difference. If I1 and I2 differ
numerically, then they differ in the respect of being different entities. This respect is a property—
the property of being this entity rather than that one. And if they differ in this property, then
they are not qualitatively identical. The distinction between numerical and qualitative difference
collapses.



16.4.5       The Distinction from Cloning and Teleportation

The framework’s account of non-duplicability has important consequences for the classical puz-
zles of cloning and teleportation.

Cloning. A clone is not “you”—it is a new entity with your genetic pattern. The clone has its
own identity, its own experiences, its own future. What is duplicated is your genetic pattern,
not your identity.

Teleportation. The teleportation puzzle asks: if a machine scans your body, destroys it, and
builds a perfect copy on Mars, is the Mars person “you”? The framework dissolves this puzzle.
The Mars copy is not “you”—it is a new entity with your pattern. If the Earth copy is destroyed,
then “you” have ceased to exist in the material context, and a new entity has come into being.
The Mars copy is a new expression of a pattern that was reconstructed from your material
manifestation, but not of your identity. The Mars copy has its own identity, its own history, its
own future.

Fission. The fission puzzle asks: if a person splits into two, which one is the original? The
framework dissolves this puzzle. Neither is the original—both are new entities. The original
identity has ceased to express itself in the material context; two new identities have come into
being.

These consequences may seem counterintuitive, but they follow from the framework’s account
of identity. Identity is not a pattern that can be copied; it is an invariant structure that is
expressed in a specific context. When the context changes, the identity is not duplicated; it is
either conserved (if the same identity continues to express itself) or replaced (if a new identity
comes into being).
16.5. The Classical Puzzles of Personal Identity                                              183


16.5     The Classical Puzzles of Personal Identity
The framework’s account of rigidity, conservation, and non-duplicability dissolves several classi-
cal puzzles of personal identity.


16.5.1    Locke’s Memory Criterion
Locke defined personal identity as continuity of consciousness and memory. But we forget most
of our lives; Alzheimer’s patients lose memory. The Axiom of Identity Conservation dissolves
this puzzle. Memory is a manifestation—an expression—not identity. Even if all memory is lost,
the identity is conserved.

This dissolution has important implications for the ethics of dementia care. If personal identity
is conserved even in the absence of memory, then the person with advanced dementia is still
the same person—with the same rights, the same dignity, and the same claim to care. The
dissolution of the Lockean puzzle is therefore not just a theoretical matter; it has practical
ethical consequences.


16.5.2    Reid’s Problem
Reid argued that personal identity cannot be merely memory—it must be a continuous existence
through time. The Axiom of Identity Conservation supports this view.

Reid’s problem was that memory is discontinuous—we forget, we sleep, we lose consciousness.
If personal identity were merely memory, then it would be interrupted every time we sleep.
Reid concluded that personal identity must be something more than memory—a continuous
existence that underlies the discontinuities of consciousness. The Axiom of Identity Conservation
vindicates Reid’s insight: identity is conserved continuously, even when its manifestations are
interrupted.


16.5.3    The Gradual Replacement Puzzle
The gradual replacement puzzle asks: if a person’s cells are gradually replaced over time, at
what point does the person cease to be the same person? The Axiom of Identity Conservation
dissolves this puzzle. The identity is conserved throughout the process, because the identity is
not the cells—it is the invariant structure that governs them.

This dissolution has important implications for our understanding of aging. Aging involves the
gradual replacement of cells, the gradual change of appearance, the gradual transformation of
capacities. But the identity of the person is conserved throughout. The aging person is the same
person—with the same history, the same relationships, the same rights.


16.6     Objections and Replies
Objection 16.1. Rigidity is incompatible with the manifest fact of change. If identity is rigid,
how can anything change?
184                          Chapter 16. Identity Rigidity, Conservation, and Non-Duplicability


Reply 16.1. Rigidity and change are not opposed; they are complementary. Identity is rigid
precisely so that change can be intelligible as the change of a single entity. The rigidity of identity
is the condition of possibility for change, not its enemy. Without rigidity, change would be a
sequence of unrelated events, not the change of a persisting thing.

Objection 16.2. Rigidity is a form of essentialism, which has been discredited by modern
biology and philosophy.

Reply 16.2. No. Essentialism posits a fixed set of properties that a thing must have to be what
it is. Rigidity posits a pattern of invariance that persists through change. The difference is that
essence is static, while rigidity is dynamic—it is defined relative to a class of transformations,
not to a fixed set of properties. A thing can change all its properties and still remain the same,
provided the change is within the class of allowable transformations.

Objection 16.3. If identity is rigid, then there is no room for genuine novelty or creativity.
Everything is predetermined by the identity’s structure.

Reply 16.3. This objection conflates rigidity with determinism. Rigidity is a property of
identity, not of manifestation. The manifestations of an identity are not predetermined by the
identity; they are constrained by it, but they also depend on the context. Within the constraints
imposed by the identity, there is room for novelty and creativity. The identity determines the
space of possible manifestations, but not the specific manifestation that occurs in a given context.

Objection 16.4. Conservation is incompatible with radical change. If a person changes radi-
cally, how can their identity be conserved?

Reply 16.4. Conservation is compatible with radical change, because conservation is at the
level of identity, not manifestation. A person can change radically in their manifestation while
their identity remains conserved. The expression may change, but the identity that expresses
itself remains the same.

Objection 16.5. The transcendental argument only shows that conservation is presupposed by
our experience, not that it holds in reality.

Reply 16.5. This is correct, and we accept it. The argument is not a proof from a God’s-eye
view; it is a transcendental deduction. It shows that conservation is a condition of possibility of
finite inquiry into identity. This is consistent with Axiom 0.22—the philosopher, too, is subject
to the limits of finite inquiry.

Objection 16.6. Duplication is physically possible. We can clone organisms, copy information,
and build replicas.

Reply 16.6. Duplication of manifestation is physically possible; duplication of identity is not.
What is duplicated in cloning, copying, and replicating is the pattern—the set of observable
properties. But the pattern is not the identity. The pattern is an expression of the identity;
duplicating the pattern is producing a new expression, not duplicating the identity.

Objection 16.7. The direct argument for non-duplicability assumes that two distinct entities
must differ in some respect. But what if they differ only numerically, not qualitatively?
16.7. Conditions of Revision and Falsification                                                             185


Reply 16.7. Numerical difference is itself a respect in which two entities differ. If I1 and I2 differ
numerically, then they differ in the respect of being different entities. This respect is sufficient to
break the identity relation. Moreover, with the Theory of Expression, numerical difference is a
difference in expression—two identities that express themselves in different contexts are different
identities, even if their patterns are similar.

Objection 16.8. The Principle of Identity of Indiscernibles is controversial and cannot be
assumed.

Reply 16.8. The principle is adopted as a working assumption, not proven. If a critic rejects the
principle, the direct argument for non-duplicability does not go through—but neither does the
possibility of genuine duplication. The choice is between accepting the principle and accepting
that identity can be duplicated. The framework chooses the former, in line with its Theory of
Expression: if identity is expression, then two entities that differ only numerically differ in their
expression, and therefore in their identity.

Objection 16.9. The dissolution of the teleportation puzzle seems to imply that teleportation
is always a form of death. This is a disturbing conclusion.

Reply 16.9. The conclusion is indeed disturbing, but it follows from the framework. If telepor-
tation involves destroying the original and creating a copy, then it is a form of death followed
by creation—not transportation. This is a conclusion that some philosophers (like Parfit) have
been willing to accept, and it has important implications for the ethics of emerging technologies.
The framework does not shy away from this conclusion; it accepts it as a consequence of its
commitment to non-duplicability.




16.7       Conditions of Revision and Falsification

    Conditions of Revision and Falsification.          What would count against the claims of
    this chapter.

     • Against the (T) argument from logical necessity: a coherent account of identity that admits
       of degrees without losing the concept of persistence.

     • Against the (T) transcendental argument for conservation: a demonstration that temporal
       experience is possible without conservation (i.e., that memory, anticipation, and recognition
       do not presuppose a persisting subject).

     • Against the (T) direct argument for non-duplicability: a demonstration that two numerically
       distinct entities can be qualitatively identical without violating the concept of identity (i.e.,
       that numerical difference is not itself a qualitative difference).

     • Against the (A) Principle of Identity of Indiscernibles as a working assumption: a demon-
       stration that the principle is either incoherent or unnecessary for the framework.

     • Against the (T) dissolution of the classical puzzles: a demonstration that one of the puzzles
       cannot be dissolved by the framework’s account, or that the dissolution generates more
       problems than it solves.

16.8        Conclusion: The Structural Core of Identity
This chapter has developed three structural properties of identity: rigidity, conservation, and
non-duplicability. These properties constitute the structural core of the framework’s account of
identity.

We have seen that identity is rigid: it is invariant under all transformations of its manifestations.
We have seen that identity is conserved: it is invariant under all temporal transformations of
its manifestations. We have seen that identity is non-duplicable: it cannot be copied, because
duplication would require two entities that are the same. And we have seen that these three prop-
erties dissolve several classical puzzles of personal identity—Locke’s memory criterion, Reid’s
problem, gradual replacement, cloning, teleportation, and fission.

The next chapter will develop Pure Relationality—the doctrine that ownership, belonging, and
territoriality are relational edges, not essential properties.

   Epistemic Status of This Chapter. Main claims and their status. Axiom 0.4 (Pure

Keywords: Pure Relationality, Ownership, Belonging, Territoriality, Relational Edges, Graph
