25.1        Introduction: The Missing Question
Why should identity persist at all? What makes the preservation of invariant structure through
manifestational flux a good? This chapter addresses the teleological and axiological foundations
of viability. And it introduces a radical thesis: ethics is not a human invention; it is a discovery.

The question is not idle. Many philosophical traditions have denied that persistence is a good.
For the nihilist, nothing matters—including persistence. For the existentialist, persistence is
a burden—the self must be overcome. For the Buddhist, the attachment to persistence is the
root of suffering. The philosophy of viability must address these challenges if it is to claim that
274                                         Chapter 25. Viability as the Supreme Ontological Virtue


viability is a virtue.

But with the Theory of Expression (Chapter 12), we can reframe the question. Why should
identity persist? Because identity is its expression, and to persist is to continue expressing. The
good of persistence is the good of expression—the good of an identity continuing to bring forth
its manifestations, to actualize its structure, to find itself in the world. Viability is not merely
a descriptive fact about how systems persist; it is the success of expression—the achievement of
an identity in expressing itself without losing itself in the process.

The chapter proceeds in seven stages. First, it diagnoses the crisis of teleology in modern
philosophy. Second, it develops the positive account of viability as an ontological virtue—as the
success of expression. Third, it addresses the challenge of Hume’s Guillotine. Fourth, it presents
the section “Why Viability and Not X?”—the framework’s most direct comparison with rival
axiological frameworks. Fifth, it develops the topology of possible collapse and the constellation
of threat. Sixth, it develops the gradient from survival to flourishing, and the principle of
requisite variety. Seventh, it addresses objections.



25.2        The Crisis of Teleology in Modern Philosophy

25.2.1       Hume’s Guillotine

The modern philosophical tradition, beginning with David Hume, erected a strict barrier be-
tween descriptive statements (what “is”) and normative statements (what “ought” to be).1 This
observation—later dubbed “Hume’s Guillotine”—became a foundational axiom of modern ethics:
no set of purely factual premises can logically entail a normative conclusion.

Hume’s Guillotine has profound consequences for any attempt to ground ethics in metaphysics.
If no factual premise can entail a normative conclusion, then no metaphysical claim—including
the claim that identity is conserved—can by itself establish an ethical claim—including the claim
that conservation is good. The philosophy of viability must therefore address Hume’s challenge
directly.



25.2.2       Nietzsche and the Death of Transcendent Value

If Hume severed fact from value, Friedrich Nietzsche severed value from any transcendent an-
chor.2 The combined force of Hume’s Guillotine and Nietzsche’s radical perspectivism left mod-
ern philosophy in a state of axiological paralysis.

Nietzsche’s challenge is even more radical than Hume’s. Hume asks: how can we derive values
from facts? Nietzsche asks: why should we value anything at all? If there is no transcendent an-
chor for value, then all values are human creations—and can be created differently or abandoned
altogether.

  1
      David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1978), Book III.
  2
      Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science, trans. Walter Kaufmann (New York: Vintage Books, 1974).
25.3. Viability as Ontological Virtue                                                               275


25.2.3     The Pragmatic Retreat

Faced with this paralysis, contemporary philosophy of science and ethics has largely retreated
to pragmatism. Viability is treated as a useful heuristic, but not as a genuine ontological or
axiological category.

The pragmatic retreat is a form of surrender. It concedes that there is no objective ground for
value, and settles for what “works.” But this surrender is unsatisfactory. If viability is merely a
useful heuristic, then there is no reason to prefer a viable system to a non-viable one, except by
arbitrary preference.

The philosophy of viability rejects this pragmatic retreat. It argues that viability is not merely
a useful heuristic; it is a genuine ontological virtue—the success of expression. And it argues
that ethics is not a human invention; it is a discovery of the structure of expression.


25.3      Viability as Ontological Virtue
Axiom 0.12 (Viability as Ontological Virtue). (A)Viability—the capacity of an identity
to maintain its structural continuity through the flux of its manifestations—is the supreme
ontological virtue, the transcendental condition of all value.


25.3.1     The Reinterpretation of Viability as the Success of Expression

In the original framework, viability was defined as “the capacity of an identity to maintain its
structural continuity through the flux of its manifestations.” With the Theory of Expression, we
can give a more precise account: viability is the success of expression.

      Viability is the success of expression: the capacity of an identity to express itself in
      its manifestations without losing itself in them.

Why is this reinterpretation important? Because it connects viability to the Theory of Expres-
sion. Viability is not merely a matter of maintaining structure; it is a matter of expressing
structure. The viable identity is the one that can express itself fully—in all its manifestations—
without being overwhelmed by them.

This reinterpretation also clarifies the relationship between viability and love. Love is the force
that returns manifestation to its source (Chapter 19). Viability is the success of this return—the
capacity of the identity to express itself and to receive the return of its expression. Viability and
love are thus intimately connected: love is the force, viability is the success.


25.3.2     The Aristotelian Recovery

To understand why viability is a good, we must recover the concept of arete (virtue or excellence).
For Aristotle, the virtue of a thing is the structural excellence that enables the thing to fulfill
its function.3 The virtue of an identity is viability—its capacity to express itself successfully.
  3
   Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, in The Complete Works of Aristotle: The Revised Oxford Translation, ed.
Jonathan Barnes (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1984).
276                                      Chapter 25. Viability as the Supreme Ontological Virtue


This recovery has an important consequence. If virtue is structural excellence, then virtue is not
a matter of opinion or preference; it is a matter of structure. A thing is virtuous to the extent
that its structure enables it to fulfill its function. The virtue of a knife is sharpness; the virtue
of an eye is clear vision; the virtue of an identity is viability—the success of its expression.

This does not mean that virtue is “objective” in the sense of being independent of all observers.
It means that virtue is structural —it is a feature of the thing’s structure, not of the observer’s
preferences.


25.3.3      The Argument from Ontological Priority

The argument for viability as the ultimate good proceeds as follows:

1. All values (moral, aesthetic, epistemic, practical) presuppose the existence of entities that
      hold, perceive, or enact those values.

2. The existence of an entity, over time and through change, presupposes the persistence of its
      invariant identity—that is, the success of its expression.

3. The success of expression is precisely what we have defined as viability.

4. Therefore, viability is the ontological precondition of all values.

5. A precondition of all values cannot itself be value-neutral; it is the supreme structural good
      upon which all other goods depend.

The argument is valid in form. But it has a gap—the gap between “X is a precondition of Y” and
“X is a good.” This gap is precisely Hume’s Guillotine. The argument establishes that viability
is a precondition of value; it does not establish that viability is valuable.


25.3.4      A Note on the Limits of the Transcendental Argument

We must be precise about what the transcendental argument does and does not establish. It
demonstrates that viability is a structural precondition of all normative discourse. But this is
not yet to say that viability is itself a normative good. There is a logical gap between “X is
necessary for Y” and “X is valuable.”

To bridge this gap, we must make explicit an axiom that the transcendental argument alone
cannot furnish: the axiom that the conditions of possibility of value are themselves value-bearing.
This axiom is not derived from the structure of being; it is a choice ((A)).

This is not a derivation of “ought” from “is.” It is a transcendental-pragmatic argument: the
denial of viability’s value is self-undermining because it presupposes the very viability it denies.

We acknowledge that this move will not satisfy all critics. A strict Humean may object that the
axiom is itself a normative premise, and therefore the argument is circular. We accept this charge
in part: the argument does not prove that viability is a good from purely descriptive premises.
(This is the framework’s most honest statement of the limits of its axiological argument, and it
is why the section “Why Viability and Not X?” below is offered as a comparison of frameworks
rather than as a demonstration.)
25.4. Why Viability and Not X?                                                                    277


25.3.5     The Pragmatic Argument for Viability
To supplement the transcendental argument, we offer a pragmatic argument. Consider what
happens when someone denies that viability is valuable. They must still act—they must still
make choices, pursue goals, and maintain their existence. But in acting, they presuppose their
own viability. They presuppose that they will continue to exist as the same agent, capable of
making and executing choices. The denial of viability’s value is therefore performatively self-
undermining: it cannot be consistently enacted.

But with the Theory of Expression, we can deepen this. To act is to express oneself. Every action
is an expression of the agent’s identity. And every expression presupposes the viability of the
agent—the capacity of the agent to express itself without losing itself in the process. The denial
of viability’s value is therefore not merely performatively self-undermining; it is expressively
self-undermining. It denies the very condition that makes expression possible.

This pragmatic argument is not a proof. It is a reductio of the denial of viability’s value. It
shows that the denial is not a live option—that anyone who acts must implicitly affirm the value
of viability.


25.4      Why Viability and Not X?
The argument so far has established that viability is a structural precondition of value. It has
not established that viability is the supreme value—that it is to be preferred to rival axiological
foundations. A critic is entitled to ask: why viability, and not one of the other candidates
that the history of ethics has proposed? This section addresses that question directly. It is the
framework’s most direct response to the charge of arbitrary axiological foundationalism.


25.4.1     The Rival Frameworks
We consider five rival axiological foundations, each of which has serious defenders in the history
of philosophy. For each, we state (i) its central claim, (ii) its strengths, (iii) its weaknesses as a
foundational commitment, and (iv) how the framework’s commitment to viability compares.


Hedonism (Bentham, Mill, contemporary utilitarians)

Central claim. The supreme value is pleasure (or the satisfaction of preferences, in contempo-
rary versions), and the right action is the one that maximizes it.

Strengths. Hedonism has a clear criterion of value, a measurable quantity (pleasure, preference
satisfaction), and a powerful normative imperative (the greatest good for the greatest number).
It has been the dominant axiology of modern welfare economics and public policy.

Weaknesses. Hedonism has been criticized on three grounds. (i) The experience machine
objection (Nozick): if pleasure were the supreme value, we should prefer a machine that produces
the experience of pleasure to real life; but we do not. (ii) The problem of adaptive preferences:
if pleasure is the measure, then a person who has been socially conditioned to prefer a restricted
life may be counted as better off than a person who has not, which seems unjust. (iii) The
278                                      Chapter 25. Viability as the Supreme Ontological Virtue


incommensurability problem: pleasures of different kinds (physical, intellectual, aesthetic) are
not obviously commensurable, and the attempt to make them commensurable has seemed to
many to distort what is valuable about them.

Comparison with viability. Viability is not a quantity to be maximized; it is a structural
condition of successful expression. It does not suffer from the experience machine objection,
because it is not about the experience of pleasure but about the capacity to express oneself in
one’s manifestations. It does not suffer from the adaptive preference problem in the same way,
because it is not about what a person prefers but about whether the person can express their
invariant structure. It does not suffer from the incommensurability problem, because it is not
a measure of quantity but a structural criterion. Whether these are advantages depends on
whether one finds the hedonist’s criterion attractive; the framework’s claim is that viability is
the more explanatory foundation, not that hedonism is refuted.


Kantian Autonomy (Kant, Korsgaard, contemporary constructivists)

Central claim. The supreme value is autonomy—the capacity to give oneself the moral law.
The right action is the one that respects the autonomy of all rational agents.

Strengths. Kantian autonomy has a clear criterion of value (the categorical imperative), a
powerful normative imperative (the kingdom of ends), and a strong protection of individual
dignity. It has been the dominant axiology of modern human rights discourse.

Weaknesses. Kantian autonomy has been criticized on three grounds. (i) The problem of non-
rational beings: if autonomy is the supreme value, then beings who are not autonomous (infants,
the severely cognitively disabled, non-human animals) have no intrinsic moral standing. (ii) The
problem of moral luck: if autonomy is the supreme value, then the outcomes of action matter
less than the maxims behind them, which has seemed to many to ignore the real suffering that
actions cause. (iii) The problem of abstraction: the categorical imperative is a formal criterion,
and its application to concrete situations has seemed to many to be indeterminate.

Comparison with viability. Viability does not suffer from the problem of non-rational beings,
because it is a structural feature of every identity, not only of rational agents. It does not suffer
from the problem of moral luck, because it is about the success of expression, not only about
the maxims behind action. It does not suffer from the problem of abstraction in the same way,
because the ethical mechanics of the Hubs (Chapter 26) provides a concrete structural framework
for ethical discovery. The framework’s claim is that viability is the more inclusive foundation,
not that Kantian autonomy is refuted.


The Capabilities Approach (Sen, Nussbaum)

Central claim. The supreme value is the capability to function in a set of central human ways
(life, health, bodily integrity, senses, imagination, thought, emotions, practical reason, affiliation,
other species, play, control over one’s environment). The right action is the one that promotes
these capabilities.

Strengths. The capabilities approach has a rich, pluralistic criterion of value, a powerful
25.4. Why Viability and Not X?                                                                        279


normative imperative (the promotion of human flourishing), and a strong empirical grounding
in development economics and human rights. It has been the dominant axiology of contemporary
development theory.

Weaknesses. The capabilities approach has been criticized on two grounds. (i) The problem
of the list: the list of central capabilities is not derived from a single principle; it is a historically
contingent construction, and different theorists have proposed different lists. (ii) The problem
of the threshold: the approach does not specify how the capabilities are to be weighed against
one another, or what to do when they conflict.

Comparison with viability. Viability is not a list of capabilities; it is a structural condition
of successful expression. It does not suffer from the problem of the list in the same way, because
it is not a list but a criterion (the success of expression). It does not suffer from the problem of
the threshold in the same way, because the ethical mechanics of the Hubs provides a structural
framework for resolving conflicts (the ethics of measure, meaning, and manifestation). The
framework’s claim is that viability is the more fundamental foundation, not that the capabilities
approach is refuted.

Care Ethics (Gilligan, Noddings, Held)

Central claim. The supreme value is care—the maintenance of relationships of mutual concern.
The right action is the one that sustains and enhances these relationships.

Strengths. Care ethics has a relational criterion of value, a powerful normative imperative
(the priority of the concrete other over the abstract rule), and a strong empirical grounding in
the ethics of family, friendship, and community. It has been a corrective to the abstraction of
Kantian and utilitarian ethics.

Weaknesses. Care ethics has been criticized on two grounds. (i) The problem of scope: care
ethics has been accused of being unable to address distant others, institutions, and impersonal
obligations. (ii) The problem of justification: care ethics has been accused of lacking a principled
criterion for distinguishing good care from bad.

Comparison with viability. Viability is deeply relational: the ethical mechanics of the Hubs
(Chapter 26) and the concept of topological integrity (Chapter 29) are explicitly relational. But
viability is not limited to intimate relations; it is a structural feature of every identity, including
distant others and institutions. And it provides a principled criterion (the success of expression)
for distinguishing good care from bad. The framework’s claim is that viability is the more
general foundation, not that care ethics is refuted.

Aristotelian Virtue Ethics (Aristotle, MacIntyre, Foot)

Central claim. The supreme value is eudaimonia—human flourishing, the excellent activity of
the soul in accordance with virtue. The right action is the one that a person of practical wisdom
would choose.

Strengths. Virtue ethics has a rich, holistic criterion of value, a powerful normative imperative
(the development of character), and a strong empirical grounding in the virtues of particular
280                                     Chapter 25. Viability as the Supreme Ontological Virtue


traditions. It has been the dominant axiology of classical and medieval ethics.

Weaknesses. Virtue ethics has been criticized on two grounds. (i) The problem of the virtues:
the list of virtues is not derived from a single principle, and different traditions have proposed
different lists. (ii) The problem of the criterion: virtue ethics does not provide a decision
procedure for resolving moral dilemmas.

Comparison with viability. Viability is a natural ally of virtue ethics: the framework explic-
itly recovers the concept of arete (§25.3). But viability is not a list of virtues; it is a structural
condition of successful expression. It does not suffer from the problem of the virtues in the same
way, because it is not a list but a criterion. It does not suffer from the problem of the criterion
in the same way, because the ethical mechanics of the Hubs provides a structural framework for
resolving dilemmas. The framework’s claim is that viability is the more general foundation of
which the virtues are manifestations, not that virtue ethics is refuted.


25.4.2    The Framework’s Comparative Claim

The framework does not claim to have refuted any of these rival frameworks. It claims that
viability is the more coherent, more explanatory, and more fruitful foundational commitment,
for three reasons.

First, viability is more general. Hedonism applies only to sentient beings; Kantian autonomy
applies only to rational agents; the capabilities approach applies only to humans (or, at most, to
animals with similar capacities); care ethics applies primarily to intimate relationships. Viability
applies to every identity—human, animal, artificial, or divine—because every identity expresses
itself and every expression is subject to the requirements of viability.

Second, viability is more fundamental. Hedonism, Kantian autonomy, the capabilities
approach, and care ethics all presuppose the existence of an entity that has the relevant capacity
(to feel pleasure, to be autonomous, to function, to care). The existence of such an entity,
over time and through change, presupposes the persistence of its invariant identity—that is, the
success of its expression. Viability is thus the condition of possibility of the other frameworks,
not a rival to them.

Third, viability is more fruitful. The framework’s concept of viability generates a rich set
of structural concepts (the ethical mechanics of the Hubs, the topology of possible collapse, the
constellation of threat, the principle of requisite variety) that have been developed in Parts VI–
VII and that are oriented toward the science and technology of viability (Appendices A–E). The
rivals have their own rich traditions, but the framework’s claim is that viability generates more
fruitful inquiry for the specific problem the framework addresses (the persistence of identity
through change).


25.4.3    The Acknowledged Limitation

The framework acknowledges that this comparison is not a proof. It is a comparative argument
((T)), and its conclusion (that viability is the more coherent, more explanatory, more fruitful
foundation) is a commitment ((A)). A reader who weighs the considerations differently and
25.5. The Topology of Possible Collapse                                                          281


prefers a rival foundation is not refuted; they are simply operating within a different framework.
The framework’s claim is that the comparison is fair and honest, not that it is decisive.




25.5     The Topology of Possible Collapse

25.5.1    The Ontological Precedence of Danger

In classical risk theory, danger is understood as a conjunction of probability and magnitude. The
philosophy of viability proposes a deeper understanding. Before a danger can be probable or
severe, it must first be possible. And possibility is not an empirical category; it is an ontological
one.

This insight has important consequences for risk assessment. Classical risk theory focuses on
the probability of a hazard—how likely it is to occur. The philosophy of viability focuses on the
possibility of a hazard—whether the structure of the system permits the hazard to propagate
from a source to a critical identity node.




25.5.2    The Primacy of Structure over Statistics

The ontological possibility of destruction precedes its empirical occurrence. A bridge does not
become dangerous when the probability of collapse exceeds a threshold; it becomes dangerous
the moment its structural topology permits a propagation path from a hazard source to a critical
identity node.

This means that structural analysis is prior to statistical analysis. We must first understand the
topology of possible collapse—the pathways along which hazards can propagate—before we can
meaningfully assess the probability of collapse. Statistics without topology is blind.




25.5.3    The Three Dimensions of Structural Vulnerability

The framework distinguishes three dimensions of structural vulnerability.

1. Reachability: Is there a connected pathway from the hazard source to the identity core?

2. Multiplicity: How many independent pathways exist?

3. Depth: How many layers of manifestation must the hazard traverse before reaching the
   invariant identity?

These three dimensions define the Structural Vulnerability of an identity. A system with high
reachability, high multiplicity, and low depth is highly vulnerable. A system with low reachability,
low multiplicity, and high depth is highly resilient. (A fourth dimension, expressivity, is added
in Appendix A.)
282                                         Chapter 25. Viability as the Supreme Ontological Virtue


25.6       The Constellation of Threat

25.6.1     Beyond the Substantialist Conception of Risk

Classical risk theory treats risk as a property of an object or event. The philosophy of viability
rejects this. Danger is not a property; it is a relation. More precisely, it is a constellation—
a structured relational configuration that binds together three distinct elements: a source of
disruption, a vulnerability in the identity’s structure, and a valued function whose impairment
constitutes harm.


25.6.2     The Teleological Core of the Constellation

The crucial element in the Constellation of Threat is the valued function. A threat is not a
threat unless it endangers something that matters.

This is why the axiology of viability is inseparable from the ontology of viability. To understand
what is threatened, we must understand what is valuable. And to understand what is valuable,
we must understand the structure of the identity that is at risk.


25.6.3     The Ethical Implications of the Constellation

If danger is not a property but a relational constellation, then ethical responsibility is distributed
across the entire constellation.

This distribution has important consequences. It means that responsibility for preventing harm
is not limited to the source of the hazard. It extends to everyone who participates in the
constellation—to those who maintain the vulnerable identity, to those who benefit from the
valued function, and to those who have the power to alter the configuration.


25.7       From Survival to Flourishing

25.7.1     Engineering Resilience versus Ontological Resilience

The concept of resilience conceals a crucial distinction, first articulated by C. S. Holling.4 Engi-
neering resilience is the capacity of a system to return to a single, pre-defined equilibrium after
a perturbation. Ontological resilience is the capacity of a system to persist as the same identity
across radical transformations of its manifestations.

The philosophy of viability is concerned with ontological resilience, not engineering resilience.


25.7.2     The Gradient from Survival to Flourishing

At one end of the gradient is mere survival ; at the other end is flourishing. The ultimate telos
of viability is not mere survival but flourishing.
   4
    C. S. Holling, “Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems,” Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 4
(1973): 1–23.
25.8. Requisite Variety as a Normative Principle                                                   283


But with the Theory of Expression, we can give a more precise account. Flourishing is the
perfection of expression—the full expression of an identity’s structural richness. It is not merely
the maintenance of identity, but the expansion of expression—the realization of new possibilities,
the integration of new manifestations, the deepening of structural coherence.

This gradient has important ethical implications. It means that the goal of viability is not merely
to survive, but to flourish. It means that the ethical task is not merely to prevent collapse, but
to promote the full expression of identity.



25.8      Requisite Variety as a Normative Principle

25.8.1     Ashby’s Law and Its Philosophical Significance

W. Ross Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety states that a control system must possess at least as
much internal variety as the variety of the disturbances it seeks to regulate.5 Translated into
the philosophical vocabulary of viability, this becomes: The capacity of an identity to maintain
its invariant structure is bounded by the diversity of its manifestational repertoire.

This translation has profound implications. It means that the suppression of diversity is not
merely a political or aesthetic harm; it is an ontological harm. A system that suppresses diversity
reduces its own capacity for viability—and therefore its own capacity for expression.


25.8.2     From Cybernetic Law to Ethical Imperative

The suppression of diversity is not merely a political or aesthetic harm; it is an ontological harm.
Every act of homogenization is an act of ontological violence.

This ethical imperative follows from the structural requirement. If viability requires diversity,
then the promotion of diversity is not merely a preference—it is a requirement of viability. The
ethical imperative is not derived from liberal ideology; it is derived from the structural conditions
of viability.


25.8.3     Beer’s Recursive Viability

Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model extended Ashby’s insight by demonstrating that viability
is recursively nested.6

Beer’s insight is that every viable system contains viable subsystems, and is itself contained
in a larger viable system. This recursive structure has important implications. It means that
viability at one level cannot be achieved at the expense of viability at another level. The viable
system must maintain the viability of its subsystems, and must contribute to the viability of the
larger system in which it is embedded.

    W. Ross Ashby, An Introduction to Cybernetics (London: Chapman & Hall, 1956).
   6
    Stafford Beer, Brain of the Firm (London: Allen Lane, 1972); Stafford Beer, The Heart of Enterprise
(Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, 1979).

25.9       Crossing the Bridge: From “Is” to “Ought”

25.9.1         The Transcendental Argument for Viability

1. Any normative claim (“X ought to be”) presupposes the existence of a subject capable of
      making, understanding, or enacting that claim.

2. The existence of such a subject presupposes the viability of that subject.

3. Therefore, the viability of the subject is a transcendental precondition of all normative dis-
      course.

4. A transcendental precondition of all normative discourse cannot itself be normatively neutral.

5. Therefore, viability is the supreme “ought”—the ontological good that grounds all other
      goods.


25.9.2         The Limits of the Argument

We must be honest about the limits of this argument. The transcendental argument establishes
viability as the supreme structural good. But it does not specify the content of those other
values.

The argument shows that viability is a precondition of value, but it does not show what values
should be pursued, or how conflicts between values should be resolved. These are questions for
substantive ethics, not for the metaphysics of viability.


25.9.3         The Acknowledgment of Circularity

We acknowledge that the transcendental argument has a circular aspect. The axiom that the
conditions of possibility of value are themselves value-bearing is a normative premise, not a
descriptive one. The argument therefore does not derive “ought” from “is”; it makes explicit a
normative commitment that is already implicit in normative discourse.

This is not a defect; it is a feature of any transcendental argument. Kant’s transcendental
deduction of the categories also has a circular aspect: it presupposes the possibility of experience
in order to establish the conditions of experience. The circularity is not vicious; it is the structure
of a foundational inquiry.


25.10           Objections and Replies
Objection 25.1. The transcendental argument commits the naturalistic fallacy.

Reply 25.1. The argument does not derive an “ought” from an “is.” It shows that anyone
engaged in normative discourse is already committed to the value of viability.

Objection 25.2. The Topology of Possible Collapse ignores the role of probability in risk
assessment.

Reply 25.2. It does not ignore probability; it situates it. Probability is an empirical measure
25.10. Objections and Replies                                                                   285


of how likely a structurally possible event is.

Objection 25.3. The Constellation of Threat distributes responsibility so widely that no one
is responsible.

Reply 25.3. Distributed responsibility is not the absence of responsibility. It means that
responsibility is shared among the elements of the constellation.

Objection 25.4. The imperative to promote diversity is a liberal ideology in disguise.

Reply 25.4. The imperative is derived from Ashby’s Law, not from liberal ideology. It is a
structural requirement for viability, not a political preference.

Objection 25.5. Viability is too vague a concept to ground substantive ethical obligations.

Reply 25.5. Viability is structural, not vague. It is defined as the capacity of an identity
to maintain its structural continuity—or, with the Theory of Expression, the success of its
expression. The vagueness is in the application of the concept, not in the concept itself.

Objection 25.6. If viability is a precondition of value, then it is not itself a value. It is a
condition, not a good.

Reply 25.6. The distinction between a condition and a good is not as sharp as it appears.
Conditions of possibility are themselves valuable, because without them, nothing else is possible.
The value of viability is the value of the condition that makes all other values possible.

Objection 25.7. If viability is the supreme value, then we should preserve every identity, no
matter how harmful.

Reply 25.7. Viability is the supreme structural value, but it is not the only value. The content
of ethics involves balancing the viability of different identities, and respecting other values such
as justice, dignity, and freedom. The philosophy of viability provides the foundation, not the
whole building.

Objection 25.8. The comparison in “Why Viability and Not X?” is not decisive. A hedonist,
a Kantian, a capability theorist, a care ethicist, or a virtue ethicist could accept the comparison
and still prefer their own framework.

Reply 25.8. This is correct, and the framework acknowledges it. The comparison is (T); its
conclusion is (A). The framework does not claim to have refuted the rivals; it claims to have
made a fair and honest comparison, and to have shown that viability is the more general, more
fundamental, and more fruitful foundation for the specific problem the framework addresses. A
reader who weighs the considerations differently is not refuted; they are simply operating within
a different framework.

25.11       Conditions of Revision and Falsification
      Conditions of Revision and Falsification.       What would count against the claims of
      this chapter.

      • Against the (A) Axiom of Viability as Ontological Virtue: a demonstration that viability is
        not the supreme structural value, or that a rival foundation is more coherent, more explana-
        tory, and more fruitful.

      • Against the (T) argument from ontological priority: a demonstration that values can exist
        without a subject capable of holding them, or that the persistence of the subject does not
        presuppose the success of its expression.

      • Against the (A) transcendental-pragmatic argument: a demonstration that the conditions
        of possibility of value are not themselves value-bearing (i.e., that the gap between “is” and
        “ought” cannot be bridged even pragmatically).

      • Against the (T) comparison in “Why Viability and Not X?”: a demonstration that one of the
        rival frameworks is more general, more fundamental, or more fruitful than viability.

      • Against the (A) topology of possible collapse: a demonstration that structural analysis is not
        prior to statistical analysis.

      • Against the (A) constellation of threat: a demonstration that danger is a property, not a
        relation.

      • Against the (A) requisite variety as a normative principle: a demonstration that diversity is
        not a structural requirement of viability.



25.12       Conclusion: The Horizon of Viability
The philosophy of viability has now completed its axiological task. We have argued that viability
is not merely a descriptive fact about how systems persist; it is the supreme ontological virtue,
the transcendental condition of all value.

We have seen that the crisis of teleology in modern philosophy is real, but not insurmountable.
We have developed the positive account of viability as an ontological virtue, grounded in the
structural conditions of value—and deepened by the Theory of Expression: viability is the
success of expression. We have addressed the challenge of Hume’s Guillotine, acknowledging the
gap between “is” and “ought” and bridging it with a transcendental-pragmatic argument. We
have presented the framework’s most direct comparison with rival axiological frameworks (“Why
Viability and Not X?”), and we have stated honestly its (T) status. And we have shown that the
imperative to promote diversity follows from the structural requirements of viability, not from
political ideology.

The next chapter will develop the ethical mechanics of the Hubs—the structural rules that govern
the passage of ascending light through the Immanent Edge. This will be the foundation of a
new ethics, one that is grounded in the structure of reality itself.

26.1     Introduction: From Axiology to Mechanics

In Chapter 25, we established that viability is the supreme ontological virtue, and that ethics is
the discovery of the structure of expression. But we did not yet develop the mechanics of this
discovery—the structural rules that govern how ethical action actually works.

This chapter develops those mechanics. It argues that ethics is not merely a set of abstract
principles; it is a set of structural rules that govern the passage of ascending light through the
Hubs. The Hubs are the loci of refraction where the light of the higher category becomes the
light of the lower category. Ethics—on this view—is the discipline of ensuring that this passage
is unobstructed.

The chapter has seven parts. First, it gives a more precise definition of ethics. Second, it
develops the ethical function of each Hub. Third, it develops the concept of ethical blockage (sin
as topological blockage). Fourth, it develops the concept of repentance (tawba) as the clearing of
the edge. Fifth, it shows how ethics is universal in structure and contextual in application. Sixth,
288                                              Chapter 26. The Ethical Mechanics of the Hubs


it addresses the connection between the ethical mechanics and the theory of evil (developed fully
in Chapter 28). Seventh, it addresses objections.



26.2     A More Precise Definition of Ethics

26.2.1    The Definition

The framework’s precise definition of ethics is this:

      Ethics is the set of structural rules that govern the passage of ascending light from
      the Immanent Edge to the Transcendental Edge of the Hubs.

This definition has three components.

First, ethics is a set of structural rules. It is not a set of arbitrary conventions, nor a set
of subjective preferences. It is a set of rules that are grounded in the structure of the Hubs.

Second, ethics governs the passage of ascending light. Ascending light is the light that
returns manifestation to its source. Ethics is concerned with the safe passage of this light—its
unobstructed return to the source.

Third, ethics is concerned with the passage from the Immanent Edge to the Tran-
scendental Edge. The Immanent Edge is the edge of the Hub oriented to the lower category;
the Transcendental Edge is the edge oriented to the higher category. Ethics is concerned with
the passage through the Hub—from the lower to the higher.



26.2.2    The Difference from the Earlier Formulation

The earlier formulation of ethics, in Chapter 25, was “ethics is action that increases ascending
light.” The new formulation is more precise: it specifies not just the direction of the light
(ascending) but the passage through which it must travel (from the Immanent Edge to the
Transcendental Edge).

The difference is important. The earlier formulation could be read as saying that ethics is merely
about increasing the quantity of ascending light. The new formulation says that ethics is about
ensuring the safe passage of the light through the Hub—which is a matter of structure, not just
of quantity.



26.2.3    Ethics and the Theory of Expression

The new formulation also connects ethics more directly to the Theory of Expression. Expression
is the descent of identity into manifestation; ethics is the safe return of the manifestation to its
source. The two are complementary: expression without return is dissipation; return without
expression is empty. Ethics is the discipline that ensures the balance—the safe return of the
light that has been expressed.
26.3. The Ethical Function of Each Hub                                                         289


26.3       The Ethical Function of Each Hub
Each Hub has its own specific ethical function, corresponding to its role in the architecture of
reality.


26.3.1     The Hub of Decree: The Ethics of Measure

The Hub of Decree refracts the pure unity of the First Determination into the general multiplicity
of the Structural Determination. Its ethical function is the ethics of measure.

The ethics of measure is the discipline of ensuring that the passage from unity to multiplicity
is proportionate—that the specification of unity into multiplicity is not distorted by excess or
deficiency.

The ethics of measure has three dimensions.

First, the dimension of proportion. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be
proportionate—it must preserve the unity while expressing the multiplicity. An action that over-
specifies (multiplies without preserving unity) is disproportionate. An action that under-specifies
(preserves unity without expressing multiplicity) is also disproportionate.

Second, the dimension of order. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be
ordered—it must follow the structure of the categories. An action that violates the order of
the categories (confuses the higher and the lower) is disorderly.

Third, the dimension of harmony. The specification of unity into multiplicity must be
harmonious—it must produce a multiplicity that is coherent, not chaotic. An action that pro-
duces chaos (multiplies without coherence) is disharmonious.

The traditional name for the ethics of measure is temperance—the virtue of moderation, the
avoidance of excess and deficiency.


26.3.2     The Hub of Signification: The Ethics of Meaning

The Hub of Signification refracts the general multiplicity of the Structural Determination into
the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation. Its ethical function is the ethics of
meaning.

The ethics of meaning is the discipline of ensuring that the passage from structure to meaning is
truthful —that the signification of structure into meaning is not distorted by deception or error.

The ethics of meaning has three dimensions.

First, the dimension of accuracy. The signification of structure into meaning must be
accurate—it must represent the structure as it is, not as we wish it to be. An action that
misrepresents the structure is inaccurate.

Second, the dimension of honesty. The signification of structure into meaning must be
honest—it must not conceal the structure behind a deceptive meaning. An action that conceals
the structure is dishonest.
290                                             Chapter 26. The Ethical Mechanics of the Hubs


Third, the dimension of fidelity. The signification of structure into meaning must be
faithful—it must preserve the structure through the signification. An action that betrays the
structure is unfaithful.

The traditional name for the ethics of meaning is truthfulness—the virtue of honesty, the avoid-
ance of deception and error.



26.3.3    The Hub of Realization: The Ethics of Manifestation

The Hub of Realization refracts the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation into
the material multiplicity of the Material Manifestation. Its ethical function is the ethics of
manifestation.

The ethics of manifestation is the discipline of ensuring that the passage from meaning to matter
is just—that the realization of meaning into matter is not distorted by exploitation or oppression.

The ethics of manifestation has three dimensions.

First, the dimension of fairness. The realization of meaning into matter must be fair—
it must distribute the conditions of manifestation equitably. An action that concentrates the
conditions of manifestation in the hands of a few is unfair.

Second, the dimension of care. The realization of meaning into matter must be caring—it
must attend to the needs of the entities whose manifestation is at stake. An action that ignores
the needs of others is uncaring.

Third, the dimension of sustainability. The realization of meaning into matter must be
sustainable—it must preserve the conditions of manifestation for future generations. An action
that exhausts the conditions of manifestation is unsustainable.

The traditional name for the ethics of manifestation is justice—the virtue of fairness, the avoid-
ance of exploitation and oppression.



26.3.4    The Unity of the Three Ethics

The three ethics—of measure, meaning, and manifestation—are not separate. They are three
aspects of a single ethics—the ethics of the safe passage of ascending light through the Hubs.

To see this, consider how each ethics depends on the others. The ethics of measure depends on
the ethics of meaning—because without accurate signification, the measure cannot be propor-
tionate. The ethics of meaning depends on the ethics of manifestation—because without just
distribution, the signification cannot be truthful. The ethics of manifestation depends on the
ethics of measure—because without proportionate measure, the distribution cannot be sustain-
able.

The three ethics are thus interdependent. They form a single structure—the ethical mechanics
of the Hubs.
26.4. Sin as Topological Blockage                                                               291


26.4     Sin as Topological Blockage

26.4.1    The Concept of Sin
In the framework’s vocabulary, sin is not primarily a legal or juridical concept. It is a structural
concept: sin is topological blockage—the obstruction of the passage of ascending light through
the Immanent Edge of a Hub.

When a person commits an unethical action—say, a deception (tadlis)—they create a distorted
reflection in the Hub of Realization. This distortion is a sediment—an accumulation of intra-
category light—that sits on the mirror of the Hub. The result is that the ascending light cannot
pass through the Immanent Edge and rise to the higher categories.

26.4.2    The Topological Blockage
The blockage is topological in the precise sense: it is a change in the structure of the network,
not just in the content of the manifestations. The distorted reflection is a new configuration of
the edges and nodes of the network—a configuration that blocks the passage of light.

This is why sin is not merely a moral failing; it is a structural event. The action changes the
topology of the network, and the change is real—it has consequences for the passage of light.

26.4.3    The Analogy of the Mirror
The analogy of the mirror (Chapter 23) illuminates the concept of sin. The Hub of Realization
is the mirror through which the identity’s expression is actualized in the material context. When
the mirror is clean, the light passes through it unobstructed. When the mirror is covered with
sediment, the light is blocked.

Sin is the covering of the mirror. It is not the destruction of the mirror; it is the accumulation
of sediment that prevents the mirror from reflecting the light.


26.5     Repentance as the Clearing of the Edge

26.5.1    The Concept of Repentance
The resolution of ethical blockage is the clearing of the Immanent Edge—the removal of the
obstruction that prevents the passage of ascending light. This is what the framework calls tawba
(repentance).

Repentance is not merely a feeling of regret. It is a structural process—the process of restoring
the flow of light through the Immanent Edge.

26.5.2    The Four Stages of Repentance
The structural process of repentance has four stages.

First, recognition. Recognizing the blockage—acknowledging the unethical action or the
incomplete expression.
292                                             Chapter 26. The Ethical Mechanics of the Hubs


Second, responsibility. Taking responsibility for the blockage—accepting that one’s action
has caused the obstruction.

Third, repair. Repairing the blockage—taking action to remove the obstruction, through
apology, restitution, or transformation of behavior.

Fourth, renewal. Renewing the flow—establishing new patterns of action that maintain the
flow of light.


26.5.3     The Continuous Nature of Repentance

This process is not a one-time event; it is a continuous practice. The Immanent Edge is always
vulnerable to blockage; the clearing of the edge is always a task in progress.

The continuous nature of repentance has an important implication. It means that repentance is
not a state to be achieved, but a practice to be maintained. The repentant person is not the one
who has achieved a state of purity, but the one who is continuously working to clear the edge.


26.5.4     The Connection to Sediment Management

The concept of repentance is closely connected to the concept of sediment management (Chap-
ter 21). The management of sediment is the general task of returning intra-category light to
its source; repentance is the specific task of returning the sediment that has been produced by
unethical action.

The connection is this: both are forms of clearing the edge. The management of sediment clears
the edge of the general accumulation of intra-category light; repentance clears the edge of the
specific accumulation of sediment that has been produced by unethical action. The two tasks
are complementary, not opposed.


26.6      Universal Structure and Contextual Application

26.6.1     The Universality of the Ethical Mechanics

The ethical mechanics of the Hubs are universal. They apply to all identities, in all contexts,
at all times. The ethics of measure, meaning, and manifestation are not arbitrary cultural
conventions; they are structural features of reality.

This universality has three consequences.

First, ethical disagreements are not fundamental. When two people disagree about
ethics, they are not disagreeing about the structure of ethics; they are disagreeing about the
application of that structure to a particular context. The structure is universal; the applications
are contextual.

Second, ethical progress is possible. If ethics is structural, then ethical progress is not
a matter of changing the structure—it is a matter of discovering the structure more fully and
applying it more accurately.
26.7. The Connection to the Theory of Evil                                                        293


Third, ethical truths are objective. The ethical mechanics of the Hubs are not a matter of
opinion; they are a matter of structure. They are discovered, not invented.


26.6.2    The Contextual Application of the Ethical Mechanics

But the universality of the ethical mechanics does not mean that the application is universal. The
application of the ethical mechanics is always contextual —it depends on the specific configuration
of the Hubs in a given situation.

This is the core of the distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances, which
will be developed in Chapter 27. The principles are universal—they are the structural rules of
the ethical mechanics. The instances are contextual—they are the specific applications of the
rules in particular situations.


26.7     The Connection to the Theory of Evil

26.7.1    The Place of Evil in the Framework

The ethical mechanics of the Hubs provide the framework for understanding evil. Evil is not a
separate category; it is a form of ethical blockage. When the passage of ascending light through
the Hubs is blocked, the result is evil—in the precise sense of sediment and suffering.

But the framework distinguishes two kinds of evil, which will be developed in Chapter 28:
contextual evil (the structural features of the Material Manifestation that cause suffering) and
active evil (the choices that block the passage of light). The ethical mechanics of the Hubs is
primarily concerned with active evil—the evil of choice.


26.7.2    The Promise of the Next Chapter

The next two chapters will develop the framework’s account of evil in detail. Chapter 27 will
develop the distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances. Chapter 28
will develop the distinction between contextual and active evil, and will show how the ethical
mechanics of the Hubs provides the structural framework for understanding both.


26.8     Objections and Replies
Objection 26.1. The ethical mechanics of the Hubs is a form of naturalism—it derives ethics
from the structure of reality. This is the naturalistic fallacy.

Reply 26.1. The ethical mechanics of the Hubs is not a form of naturalism. It does not derive
ethics from the structure of reality; it discovers ethics in the structure of reality. The distinction
is crucial: naturalism derives “ought” from “is”; the ethical mechanics of the Hubs discovers
“ought” in the same structure in which “is” is discovered. The structure is both descriptive and
normative—not because description entails normativity, but because the structure itself is the
locus of both.
294                                             Chapter 26. The Ethical Mechanics of the Hubs


Objection 26.2. The ethical mechanics of the Hubs is too abstract to be useful. How does it
help us decide what to do?

Reply 26.2. The ethical mechanics of the Hubs is not a decision procedure—it is a framework
for understanding what is at stake in ethical decisions. It helps us understand that ethical
decisions are not merely about following rules, but about maintaining the flow of light through
the Immanent Edge. The specific decision requires the discovery of the contextual application—
which is the subject of Chapter 27.

Objection 26.3. The concept of ethical blockage seems to imply that every unethical action is
a complete blockage. But unethical actions are often partial.

Reply 26.3. Ethical blockage is not binary; it is a matter of degree. The Immanent Edge can
be partially blocked, partially cleared. The ethics of the Hubs is not a matter of all-or-nothing;
it is a matter of the degree of blockage and the degree of clearing.

Objection 26.4. The concept of repentance as structural process seems to reduce repentance
to a mechanical procedure. This trivializes the moral experience.

Reply 26.4. The concept of repentance as structural process does not trivialize the moral
experience; it grounds it. Repentance is not less real because it has a structure; it is more real
because it has a structure. The structure is the condition of possibility of the experience—not
a substitute for it.

Objection 26.5. The universality of the ethical mechanics seems to imply that all cultures
share the same ethics.

Reply 26.5. The universality of the ethical mechanics does not imply that all cultures share the
same ethics. It implies that all cultures share the same structural rules of ethics—the ethics of
measure, meaning, and manifestation. But the applications of these rules are contextual—they
vary across cultures, contexts, and situations. The universality is in the structure; the diversity
is in the application.

26.10      Conclusion: The Foundation of Structural Ethics
The ethical mechanics of the Hubs is the foundation of a structural ethics—an ethics that is
grounded in the structure of reality itself, not in arbitrary conventions or subjective preferences.

We have seen that ethics is not merely a set of rules; it is a set of structural rules that govern the
passage of ascending light through the Hubs. We have seen that each Hub has its own ethical
function—the ethics of measure (temperance), the ethics of meaning (truthfulness), and the
ethics of manifestation (justice). We have seen that sin is topological blockage—the obstruction
of the flow of light. We have seen that repentance is the clearing of the obstruction. And we
have seen that the ethical mechanics are universal in structure but contextual in application.

The next chapter will develop the distinction between absolute principles and discoverable
instances—the distinction between the universal structure of ethics and the contextual appli-
cation of that structure.

27.1       Introduction: The Distinction
In the preceding chapter, we developed the ethical mechanics of the Hubs—the structural rules
that govern the passage of ascending light through the Immanent Edge. We saw that these rules
are universal in structure—they apply to all identities, in all contexts, at all times.

But a question remains: how do we apply these universal rules to particular situations? If the
rules are universal, how do they guide action in the concrete, contextual, and often ambiguous
situations of everyday life?

The answer is the distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances. The prin-
ciples are absolute—they are the structural rules of the Hubs, invariant and universal. But the
instances are discoverable—they are the contextual applications of the principles, which must
be discovered through attention, reconstruction, and testing.

This chapter develops this distinction. It has six parts. First, it introduces the distinction. Sec-
ond, it develops the concept of absolute principles. Third, it develops the concept of discoverable
instances. Fourth, it develops the process of ethical discovery. Fifth, it develops the example of
27.2. The Distinction                                                                           297


tadlis as the main example. Sixth, it addresses objections.


27.2         The Distinction

27.2.1       The Need for the Distinction
The distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances is needed because of an
apparent dilemma in ethics. If ethics is universal, it risks being too rigid—it cannot accommodate
the contextual nuances of particular situations. If ethics is contextual, it risks being too lax—it
cannot provide universal guidance across cultures and situations.

The distinction resolves this dilemma. The principles are universal—they provide the structural
framework for ethical action. But the instances are contextual—they require the discovery of
the particular application in a given situation. This allows ethics to be both universal and
context-sensitive.


27.2.2       The Nature of the Distinction
The distinction can be stated precisely.

Absolute principles are the structural rules of the Hubs—the ethics of measure, meaning, and
manifestation. They are universal and invariant. They do not change across cultures, contexts,
or situations. They are the structure of ethics.

Discoverable instances are the contextual applications of the principles—the specific actions
that embody the principles in a particular situation. They are contextual and variable. They
must be discovered through attention, reconstruction, and testing. They are the manifestations
of ethics.

The relation between principles and instances is the relation between identity and manifesta-
tion (Chapter 3). The principles are the invariant structure; the instances are the contextual
appearance. The principles are the identity of ethics; the instances are the manifestations of
ethics.


27.2.3       The Analogy with Mathematics
An analogy with mathematics may help. The principles of mathematics—the axioms, the
theorems—are universal and invariant. They do not change across cultures, contexts, or sit-
uations. But the applications of mathematics—the specific calculations, the specific proofs—are
contextual. They depend on the particular problem, the particular variables, the particular
context.

Similarly, the principles of ethics are universal and invariant—they are the structural rules of the
Hubs. But the applications of ethics—the specific actions, the specific decisions—are contextual.
They depend on the particular situation, the particular agents, the particular consequences.

This analogy is not perfect. Mathematics is a formal science, while ethics is a practical discipline.
But the analogy captures the essential point: the principles are universal, while the applications
298                                  Chapter 27. Absolute Principles and Discoverable Instances


are contextual.


27.3       Absolute Principles

27.3.1       The Three Absolute Principles
The absolute principles of ethics are the three structural rules of the Hubs.

1. The Principle of Measure: The specification of unity into multiplicity must be propor-
      tionate. This is the ethics of temperance—the avoidance of excess and deficiency.

2. The Principle of Meaning: The signification of structure into meaning must be truthful.
   This is the ethics of truthfulness—the avoidance of deception and error.

3. The Principle of Manifestation: The realization of meaning into matter must be just.
   This is the ethics of justice—the fair distribution of the conditions of manifestation.

These three principles are absolute—they are universal and invariant. They apply to all identities,
in all contexts, at all times. They do not change.


27.3.2       The Universality of the Principles
The universality of the principles has three aspects.

First, the principles are universal in scope. They apply to all identities—human, animal,
artificial, or divine. They are not limited to a particular species, a particular culture, or a
particular historical period.

Second, the principles are universal in content. They prescribe the same structural
requirements in all contexts—proportion in measure, truthfulness in meaning, and justice in
manifestation. The content of the principles does not vary.

Third, the principles are universal in authority. They are not optional; they are binding.
Any action that violates the principles is unethical, regardless of the culture, the context, or the
situation.


27.3.3       The Justification of the Principles
The principles are justified by their connection to the structure of reality. They are not arbitrary
conventions; they are structural features of the Hubs—the loci of refraction where the light of
the higher category becomes the light of the lower category.

The principle of measure is justified by the structure of the Hub of Decree—the locus where
unity is specified into multiplicity. The principle of meaning is justified by the structure of
the Hub of Signification—the locus where structure is signified into meaning. The principle of
manifestation is justified by the structure of the Hub of Realization—the locus where meaning
is realized into matter.

The principles are thus grounded in the structure of reality. They are not imposed from without;
they are discovered from within—from the structure of the Hubs themselves.
27.4. Discoverable Instances                                                                  299


27.4     Discoverable Instances

27.4.1    The Nature of Instances

If the principles are universal, how can they guide action in particular situations? The answer
is the instances—the specific applications of the principles in particular contexts.

An instance is not a mere application of a principle; it is a discovery of the principle in a
particular situation. The discovery requires attention, reconstruction, and testing—the same
process by which identity is reconstructed from manifestation (Chapter 3).


27.4.2    The Contextuality of Instances

Instances are contextual—they depend on the specific configuration of the Hubs in a given
situation. This contextuality has three aspects.

First, the contextuality of measure. What counts as proportionate specification depends
on the context—on the particular unity being specified, the particular multiplicity into which it
is specified, and the particular relations between them.

Second, the contextuality of meaning. What counts as truthful signification depends on
the context—on the particular structure being signified, the particular meaning into which it is
signified, and the particular relations between them.

Third, the contextuality of manifestation. What counts as just realization depends on
the context—on the particular meaning being realized, the particular matter into which it is
realized, and the particular relations between them.

The contextuality of instances does not undermine the universality of the principles. It simply
acknowledges that the principles must be applied differently in different contexts—that the
discovery of the instance requires attention to the particularities of the situation.


27.5     The Process of Ethical Discovery

27.5.1    The Three Stages of Discovery

The discovery of instances involves three stages, which correspond to the three stages of recon-
struction (Chapter 19).

First, attention. Attending to the manifestations of the principle in the particular situation.
This requires opening oneself to the situation, observing the relevant factors, and listening to
the voices of those involved.

Second, reconstruction. Reconstructing the principle from the manifestations in the situation.
This requires identifying the structural pattern that the principle requires in the situation, and
articulating it in a way that is clear and actionable.

Third, testing. Testing the reconstruction against new manifestations, revising it as neces-
sary. This requires acting on the reconstruction, observing the consequences, and adjusting the
300                                 Chapter 27. Absolute Principles and Discoverable Instances


reconstruction in the light of the consequences.

This process is not a linear sequence; it is a spiral—each stage informs the others, and the
process is repeated as the situation evolves.


27.5.2     The Criteria of Adequacy
The reconstruction of an instance can be more or less adequate. Its adequacy is measured by the
same criteria that govern all reconstructions (Chapter 3): consistency, stability, and fruitfulness.

Consistency. The reconstruction must be consistent with the principle—it must embody the
principle in a way that is coherent with the principle’s structure.

Stability. The reconstruction must be stable—it must not change radically in response to minor
changes in the situation.

Fruitfulness. The reconstruction must be fruitful—it must lead to actions that maintain the
flow of ascending light through the Immanent Edge.


27.6      The Example of Tadlis

27.6.1     The Concept of Tadlis
The concept of tadlis (deception, fraud; the concealment of a defect) is the framework’s main
example of the distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances.

The principle is absolute: the condemnation of tadlis. It is a structural rule of the Hub of
Realization—the rule that the signification of structure into meaning must be truthful, that the
realization of meaning into matter must be just. The rule is invariant: it applies to all identities,
in all contexts, at all times.

But the instances of tadlis are discoverable: what counts as tadlis in accounting, in medicine,
in law, in judgment—these are specific applications that require the discovery of the principle
in the particular context.


27.6.2     The Instances of Tadlis
The instances of tadlis are various, depending on the context.

In accounting. Tadlis is the concealment of a financial defect—the misrepresentation of the
financial state of an entity. The instance is discovered by attending to the specific practices of
accounting—the standards, the expectations, the legal requirements.

In medicine. Tadlis is the concealment of a medical defect—the misrepresentation of the
patient’s state, or the concealment of a risk, or the misrepresentation of a treatment’s efficacy.
The instance is discovered by attending to the specific practices of medicine—the standards of
care, the expectations of patients, the legal requirements.

In law. Tadlis is the concealment of a legal defect—the misrepresentation of a contract, or the
concealment of a fact material to a case. The instance is discovered by attending to the specific
27.7. Objections and Replies                                                                    301


practices of law—the standards of professional conduct, the expectations of clients, the legal
requirements.

In judgment. Tadlis is the concealment of a defect in judgment—the misrepresentation of the
evidence, or the concealment of a bias, or the misrepresentation of a legal principle. The instance
is discovered by attending to the specific practices of judgment—the standards of impartiality,
the expectations of the parties, the legal requirements.


27.6.3     The Discovery of the Instance
The discovery of the instance of tadlis requires the three stages of ethical discovery.

First, attention. We attend to the specific practices of the field—the standards, the expecta-
tions, the legal requirements. We observe what counts as tadlis in that field.

Second, reconstruction. We reconstruct the principle in the specific context—we articulate
what the condemnation of tadlis requires in that field.

Third, testing. We test the reconstruction against new situations—we act on it, observe the
consequences, and adjust it as necessary.


27.6.4     The Importance of the Example
The example of tadlis is important because it shows how the distinction between absolute princi-
ples and discoverable instances works in practice. The principle is absolute—it does not change.
But the instances are discoverable—they require the labor of attention, reconstruction, and
testing.

This is why the framework can say that ethics is both universal and contextual. The principle
is universal; the instance is contextual. The discovery of the instance is the labor of the ethical
agent.


27.7       Objections and Replies
Objection 27.1. If the instances are discoverable, then ethics is relative to the context. This
is a form of relativism.

Reply 27.1. The contextuality of instances does not entail relativism. The principles are
universal—they are the structural rules of the Hubs. The instances are contextual—they are
the applications of the principles in particular situations. The principles do not change; only
the applications change. This is not relativism; it is the recognition that the universal principles
must be applied differently in different contexts.

Objection 27.2. The distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances is just
a restatement of the distinction between rules and cases in casuistry.

Reply 27.2. There is a resemblance, but a crucial difference. Casuistry applies fixed rules to
particular cases. The ethics of viability does not apply fixed rules; it discovers the principle
in the light of the context. The discovery is not a mere application; it is an interpretation—a
302                                    Chapter 27. Absolute Principles and Discoverable Instances


creative, contextual, and fallible interpretation of the principle.

Objection 27.3. If the discovery of instances is creative, then it is arbitrary. Anything goes.

Reply 27.3. The discovery of instances is not arbitrary. It is constrained by the principle, by the
situation, and by the criteria of adequacy (consistency, stability, fruitfulness). The discovery is
creative, but not arbitrary—it is a disciplined creativity, guided by the structure of the principle
and the structure of the situation.

Objection 27.4. The ethics of viability does not provide a decision procedure. This makes it
useless for practical ethics.

Reply 27.4. The ethics of viability does not provide a decision procedure, but it provides a
framework for understanding what is at stake in ethical decisions—and a discipline for discover-
ing the appropriate action. The framework and discipline are not useless; they are the conditions
of possibility of responsible ethical action.

Objection 27.5. The contextuality of instances seems to imply that different cultures have
different ethics. This undermines the universality of ethics.

Reply 27.5. The contextuality of instances does not imply that different cultures have different
ethics. It implies that the same ethical principles must be applied differently in different cultural
contexts. The principles are universal; the applications are contextual. This is the strength of
the framework—it allows ethics to be both universal and context-sensitive.


27.8       Conditions of Revision and Falsification

      Conditions of Revision and Falsification.       What would count against the claims of
      this chapter.

      • Against the (A) distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances: a demon-
        stration that the distinction is either trivial or incoherent.

      • Against the (A) three absolute principles: a demonstration that there are fewer or more than
        three, or that one of them can be derived from another.

      • Against the (A) contextuality of instances: a demonstration that the instances are not con-
        textual (i.e., that the same application holds in all contexts).

      • Against the (A) three-stage process of ethical discovery: a demonstration that there are fewer
        or more than three stages, or that one stage is not necessary.




27.9       Conclusion: The Universal and the Contextual
The distinction between absolute principles and discoverable instances is the key to a structural
ethics that is both universal and context-sensitive.

We have seen that the principles of ethics are absolute—they are the structural rules of the
Hubs, universal and invariant. We have seen that the instances of ethics are discoverable—they
are the contextual applications of the principles, which must be discovered through attention,
27.9. Conclusion: The Universal and the Contextual                                                   303


reconstruction, and testing. And we have seen that the discovery of instances is not a mere
application of fixed rules; it is an interpretation of the principles in the light of the context.

This distinction allows the framework to maintain the universality of ethics while acknowledging
its contextuality. It allows ethics to be both universal and local—both one and many.

The next chapter will develop the framework’s account of evil as sediment. It will show that evil
is not a positive substance but a distortion of the network—a sediment that blocks the passage
of light. And it will distinguish between contextual evil (the structural features of the material
world) and active evil (the choices that produce sediment).
